# Foreword

Together with all our citizens, I consider it highly meaningful to compile the ten-year footsteps of the Saemaul Undong into a single volume.
While every nation is bound to have its own philosophy of history as it carves out its existence, we conceived the Saemaul Undong to seek a faster and more fruitful path toward creating history.
Although the history of the Saemaul Undong spans a mere ten years, through this movement we have not only found ways to completely sweep away the dark aspects of our past but have also nurtured the confidence that we can actively challenge the future to realize our high ideals.
Popularizing the "can-do" spirit brought about a transformation in our national lifestyle, and the collective realization that "we, too, can prosper" not only swept away the conventional mindset of accepting poverty and trials as destiny, but also enabled us to acquire the courage to wisely overcome the myriad of obstacles before us with the firm conviction that nothing is impossible when we unite, harmonize, and work together with shared strength and purpose.
People often say that history flows, but I believe history does not simply flow; rather, it is actively created along with the people who live in that era.
This is because history and humanity do not exist as separate concepts, but share an inseparable relationship, much like the two wheels of a carriage.
When we reflect on the fact that human existence without history is meaningless, and history without humanity is emptier still, we are reminded once again of the immense significance of the human beings who live through and shape their era.
How the history of the past is illuminated today is a clear yardstick that proves how the protagonists of that history lived their lives. Through the Saemaul Undong, we clearly expressed our national resolve to reflect more uprightly upon our past while devoting ourselves to the task of creating values that must be projected into the future.
6:
Through the Saemaul Undong, we clearly expressed our national resolve to devote ourselves to the task of value creation that must be projected into the future while reflecting more correctly on our past.

Our collective passion, poured into establishing an era that we can be proud of before our ancestors and proud of for our descendants, has not been in vain. Internally, we have firmly consolidated the ground upon which the sprouts of a new era can grow, while externally, we have solidly built a foundation of self-reliance that allows us to resolutely leap into any competition.

Irrespective of the era, past or present, or the region, East or West, historical outcomes have never been achieved by mere chance.

If we cannot deny the historical logic that an era unfolds brightly only when the attitude of the nation living in that era is proactive, then we cannot, for any reason, slacken the progressive attitude we have maintained so far.

In line with our national goal of building a democratic welfare society, the Saemaul Undong of the 1980s must be further vitalized. If our determination and resolve to pioneer the future are to be renewed, we must reflect on our path over the past ten years and exercise our wisdom of adopting strengths and supplementing weaknesses in order to continue making more fruitful progress.

Although this newly compiled *Ten-Year History* may not be perfect, I believe it will serve as a double-sided mirror reflecting both the past and the future.

While hoping that our citizens will widely utilize this book as a companion in their daily lives, I would like to express my deepest gratitude to the members of the writing and compilation committee who poured their hearts and souls into producing this book.

November 30, 1980

Suh Chung-hwa, Minister of Home Affairs

# Preface

Compilation Committee Chairman Kim Yoo-hyuk

To compile the first decade of the Saemaul Undong, we publish this ten-year history.

Although history connects the past and present like a great river, it is clearly the people living in that era who steer its direction.

Reflecting on our past history more dispassionately than ever before, we have struggled to pursue a brighter tomorrow.

However, the surrounding circumstances we faced did not always develop in a way that was accommodating to our position.

All kinds of trials, repeated so relentlessly as to seem heartless, sometimes swept us into despondency and despair, but our persistent efforts to overcome them always took on a proactive dynamism grounded in patience and self-restraint.

This thread of proactive dynamism, which has run unbroken throughout our national history, not only gave rise to the Saemaul Undong but was also manifested as a firm resolve to wash away accumulated historical anguish from the concrete areas of our daily lives.

Although we once regarded the future, nature, and fate as objects of fear, we have now reached a stage where we seek infinite possibilities in the future, learn the truths of wisdom and virtue from nature, and redefine our traditional fatalism through self-determination.

We stripped away the thatched roofs inherited for generations, altered the location and structure of villages once considered auspicious, and even cut through the ridges of the hills behind our villages—long believed to carry vital energy—to build roads leading to markets and distribution networks. Through such an active attitude of challenging outdated customs, we have devoted ourselves to transforming our entire way of life.

Although there was much suffering arising from the pain of self-reform and the challenge against outdated customs, the value of our earnest sweat was not in vain, laying the foundation for the everyday society of the common people, including impoverished villages, to run along the track of modernization.
8:
Although there was much pain and suffering arising from self-reform and challenging convention, the value of our warm sweat was not in vain, and a foundation was laid for grassroots society, including impoverished villages, to advance on the track of modernization.

In particular, history should not have its character defined solely by its developed outcomes; rather, greater importance must be placed on the aspect of what kind of process was undergone to achieve them.

The 10-Year Chronicle of Saemaul is a compilation of comprehensive content regarding how the tree called Saemaul has grown, what the taste of its harvested fruit is like, and how well its roots have taken hold.

Of course, it is impossible to record the entire state of development over the ten years within limited pages, but in order not to miss even the smallest detail as far as our strength allowed, we proceeded with this compilation project under the broad participation of figures from relevant fields.

Although there were many difficulties in promoting the project, thanks to the active cooperation of all participating figures, we were not only able to publish the 10-Year History in separate volumes divided into a General Overview and a Data Volume, but we also compiled the General Overview with an English summary in the appendix to serve as a reference for foreigners, and edited the major statistical data in the Data Volume by including English terminology.

Hoping that this book will be widely utilized both at home and abroad to serve as a stepping stone for establishing a more fruitful second decade, and wishing that any data not fully included here will be supplemented and published in future volumes, I write this preface on behalf of all the distinguished individuals who participated in this project.

# Chapter 1 Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong

## Section 1 Introduction

The Saemaul Undong, first proposed by President Park Chung-hee at the National Conference of Provincial Governors on April 22, 1970, has now marked a full decade of history.

An old adage says that even rivers and mountains change in ten years, and indeed, during the ten years of the Saemaul Undong, the landscape of our country has changed to an astonishing degree.

While the old saying about the changing landscape is understood to refer to natural and gradual changes—such as landslides on mountains caused by rain and snow or the shifting channels of streams—the transformation of our landscape over the ten years of the Saemaul Undong is by no means a mere natural progression.

Rather, it is a change brought about by challenging nature based on the planned and intentional objectives of our people. Therefore, the social changes achieved through the Saemaul Undong signify a development to realize our nation's yearning to "live a better life," while at the same time holding a pioneering historical significance of breaking away from complacency to establish a new foundation for our lives.

Frankly speaking, although our nation boasts a long history of five thousand years, we have lacked a distinct chapter in our history of actively challenging nature to achieve pioneering development.

In a sense, the Saemaul Undong can be described as an expression of an active attitude that revises our traditional fatalism, as we harbor dreams for the future and pursue new possibilities within nature.

This is because, having endured repeated foreign invasions and frequent domestic turmoil over a long period, we had preferred complacency to adventure, cherished the virtue of obedience over resistance, and placed greater value on passive endurance than active patience.
16:
The will to overcome based on endurance can be understood in two aspects. 

If one is an endurance premised on safety and complacency, the other is an endurance through trials that accompany the pursuit of development based on adventurous challenges. 

The Saemaul Undong clearly carries a significance characterized by the latter. 

Looking back, especially in the case of our people, it would be fair to say that the most fearsome things to humans were the future, nature, and fate. 

The foundation of our view of the future lay in the fact that no guarantees were given to us. 

Because challenging an unguaranteed future was considered a reckless act, the general mindset of trying to soothe present discontent by regressing to the past always fostered a passive attitude toward life. 

Consequently, it was true that the future was difficult to interpret as anything more than the empirical values of the past (history). 

Because nature was always an object of direct fear, it was not only difficult to escape the preconceived notion that spirits dwelled within it, but people also lacked the courage to reject the polytheistic belief that "deities are everywhere," holding onto a vague expectation that nature, through its providence of non-action, would protect the obedient human. 

Furthermore, the notion that human destiny was predetermined as innate—and that human existence, human life, and a human's entire life were harmonized within such predetermination—led people to always think of themselves as having entrusted their lives to "something" else. 

Therefore, because of the belief that human destiny is predetermined rather than forged, the general attitude toward life deepened into an even more passive and submissive state. 

However, stimuli warning us that we could no longer hesitate in such a state began to arise from both within and without. 

While the external factors involved a changing international environment where the principles of competition surged with relentless intensity, the internal factors brought about a realization that we could no longer enjoy peace and comfort while sitting upon poverty and trials.

## Chapter 1 Historical Background of the Saemaul Undong (New Village Movement)

We came to the realization that we could no longer remain complacent while mired in poverty and trials.
Here, we began to reflect on past mistakes and deeply appreciate the experiences and lessons of others.
Our outcry that "we too can live well" was clearly an expression of our conscious will and at the same time a demonstration of an active attitude.
While raising strong resistance against the resignation that had filled our minds in the past and repeatedly engaging in more proactive self-reflection against makeshift attitudes, we did not hesitate to strengthen our national determination to find a new path toward prosperity.
As a result of our agonizing efforts to find the foundation of possibility from the conditions we faced in order to realize the two supreme goals of development and security, building a foundation for development encountered the demand to find a Korean model in terms of economic development, and building a foundation for security forced us to accept the demand to strengthen our self-defense capability in terms of self-reliant national defense.
As historians point out, our past history of suffering nearly 100 challenges or invasions by other nations since the founding of Goryeo (918 AD) can be interpreted as a consequence brought about by the lethargy derived from our impoverished life, while the loss of self-defense capacity caused by that lethargy repeatedly brought the hardships of war, adding insult to injury.
However, as a result of never slacking in researching the wisest way to live through that era, we exerted our efforts to establish and promote economic development plans to build a foundation for development on one hand, and on the other hand, participated in the Vietnam War as champions of peace, generously demonstrating our commitment to contributing to the co-prosperity of mankind.
The most important shortcut to unleashing human potential and fostering an active attitude lies in setting achievable goals.
Worn down by poverty and trials, we were like travelers who had collapsed in the desert, exhausted from thirst and scorching heat, waiting for death.
However, the presentation of development goals—showing that we could reach a certain level of development in five years and live prosperously enough to envy no one in ten years through economic development plans—carried the same significance as giving hope to a traveler collapsed in the desert by showing them that an oasis lay just 50 meters ahead.
18:
...to the traveler collapsed in the desert, it was akin to offering the hope that an "oasis" lay just 50 meters ahead. 

Like a traveler exerting desperate efforts to reach an oasis, we ran toward our goal with relentless perseverance, and as a result, we came to leave behind the rewarding footprints of development, significant enough to draw global attention.

Furthermore, our experience of participating in foreign battlefields not only elevated our international status and increased our voice in the international community, but it also broadened the global horizons of many young and middle-aged citizens. Moreover, by instilling the confidence to achieve absolute victory over the enemy under any circumstances, it boosted national morale, which contributed to expanding the possibility of subduing the enemy's aggressive ambitions with the momentum of winning without fighting.

For nearly 30 years, we were able to maintain a long-term peace—unprecedented in history, though still incomplete—escaping the nightmare of the ravages of war that we had been forced to suffer on average once every seven years for over a thousand years since the founding of Goryeo.

The continuation of peace enabled continuous development in terms of construction, while the maintenance of a developmental attitude solidified our security foundation in terms of national security.

Viewed from this perspective, we cannot help but highly evaluate the immense significance of the Saemaul Undong, which contributed to providing a new momentum for historical development.

For a nation that attempts to live while burying its history, a future-oriented philosophy can hardly be articulated, and thus, its development cannot be guaranteed.

The national history of any country shares two common aspects: one is the bright side of history, and the other is the dark side of history.

While it is true that the bright side of history is infinitely proud as it instills immense pride and confidence, it is also true that the dark side of history offers a profound lesson by awakening a determination for self-reflection.

Therefore, rather than the perceived value of hiding a shameful history, it is only when we properly examine the flip side of that shameful history, take it as a lesson, and embrace it as a catalyst for a great national awakening that we can harness a far greater "energy" to accelerate development.

## Section 2: Historical Significance of the Saemaul Undong

### 1. Reflection on National History

It is a matter of great interest how future historians will evaluate the significance of the Saemaul Undong in national history and its achievements. However, no one can deny that it served as the driving force for high growth in the process of promoting Korea's modernization movement in the 1970s and became the seed for driving a spiritual revolution.

First, let us consider our geopolitical conditions. As a peninsula protruding from the Northeast Asian continent, connected to China and Siberia to the north, and close to Japan across the sea to the south, the Korean Peninsula served as a bridge between the southward-expanding forces and the northward-advancing forces. Within the dynamic correlation of these powers, the peninsula was constantly gripped by the threat and crisis of war, to the extent that there was never a day of peace.

Within the dynamic correlation of such great powers, realizing the national historical mandate of maintaining independence and unity, inheriting a single ethnic identity and a single culture, and sustaining a single state was a highly meaningful task, but also an inevitably grueling challenge.

Because a strong sense of independence for the continuous inheritance of our national history pulsated in our veins, we managed to preserve our sovereignty and survive to this day despite facing countless foreign invasions throughout history. Indeed, had it not been for our strong pride and sense of calling regarding this national independence, we might have been annexed by major powers long ago. Whenever a national crisis arose, great patriots emerged, and the people responded wisely, allowing us to rescue our national destiny from the brink of collapse—like a candle flickering in the wind—and reach the present day.

While basing ourselves on this strong spirit of independence, we nonetheless had to live while constantly ruminating on poverty as if it were our destiny. This was because our territory was small while our population was excessive. Furthermore, we had no resources to speak of, nor did we have any technological development. Because there was also no development of industries outside of agriculture, a large portion of the population had to live bound to the land.
20:
Since there was also no development of industries outside of agriculture, a large portion of the population was forced to live bound to the land. They linked production with daily life while maintaining a strong attachment to farmland and preserving kinship-based family and clan groups centered around it.

Although advanced nations had long since established the foundations of modernization and nation-state formation through Enlightenment thought and the Industrial Revolution, we lagged behind in the march toward modernization, failing to achieve either the intellectual awakening or the practical results required for it.

In the mid-Joseon Dynasty, the seeds of productive ideas and technology based on *Silsaguisi* (seeking truth from facts) were conceived by some Silhak scholars, but there was no social class to take charge of them, nor was there any group to lead them. Furthermore, there were neither the resources nor the science to link these ideas to an industrial revolution. In the midst of this, spurred by foreign invasions, an enlightenment movement arose among some pioneering intellectuals, but it faced strong resistance from conservative forces. Although the Donghak Peasant Movement was also launched by the peasantry, even that ultimately ended in failure. Ultimately, unable to have any force or group lead our modernization, we remained left behind as an underdeveloped nation. Consequently, we were forced to endure 36 years of colonial rule by Japan, which had just then emerged as a modern industrial state under the banner of enriching the nation and strengthening its military.

Under the long colonial rule, our resilient national self-consciousness erupted in resistance against Japanese imperialism. However, national unity to organize this resistance was insufficient, and we welcomed liberation in 1945 without the political capacity or economic foundation to bring their rule to an end through our own strength.

Yet even that liberation was obtained within the balance of power among superpowers, lacking the national self-reliance to direct our own independence and unification, which left us powerless to decide our own destiny. The power of the United States and the Soviet Union, which emerged in the wake of Japan's defeat, experienced a temporary cooling period after World War II, but fundamentally manifested as a pursuit of their own national interests—namely, the Far East policy of the United States and the southward expansion policy of the Soviet Union. The product of this was the stark reality of the division between North and South Korea imposed upon us. Even in that situation, as we abandoned proactive will and efforts toward national unity and unification, our own lack of capacity for national self-determination, combined with the Cold War power of external superpowers, ultimately turned the division of our nation and country into a reality.

# Chapter 1. Historical Background of Saemaul Undong

Due to the forces of the Cold War, the division of our nation and state became a reality. Furthermore, within the constraints of their Cold War system, we lacked the leeway to deviate from its trajectory, which ultimately culminated in the fratricidal tragedy of the Korean War.
As the wounds of the war were severe, post-war reconstruction presented numerous challenges. Extreme economic chaos and political instability eventually led to the April 19 Revolution and the May 16 Military Coup.

## 2. The Industrial Revolution as the Starting Point of Modernization

Saemaul Undong was a grand national leap forward, representing the first movement in our history in which the entire populace participated. The current realistic assessment is that many countries around the world cannot conceal their astonishment and envy regarding the planning, organization, leadership, drive, and achievements of Saemaul Undong.
As is well known, the world's great powers, led by Great Britain, competed to pursue industrial revolutions to build modern states based on national wealth and military strength, thereby establishing themselves as advanced nations early on.
However, the starting point of our modernization lagged approximately 200 years behind Great Britain, 150 years behind Germany, and 100 years behind Japan. We were, so to speak, in a state of historical delay.
In order to escape poverty, become a prosperous nation, cultivate national power, overcome the anxieties and crises of war through our own strength, and become a populace that could live in peace, we focused our efforts on economic development starting from the 1960s.
Our plans started virtually from nothing. All we possessed was the determination, ambition, and practice to become a nation that could live honorably and prosperously, and to build a strong and proud state. We believed that production and export were the only ways to escape poverty and prevent war, and to realize this path, the entire nation united as one around their leader. Consequently, we built factories, paved expressways, constructed ports, and built reservoirs.
In order to replicate the "Miracle on the Rhine" achieved by defeated Germany after World War II, we began to dedicate our collective, consolidated efforts to creating the "Miracle on the Han River"
22:
.
This process accelerated further in the 1970s, with Saemaul Undong serving as a catalyst for this acceleration. Leveraging the experience and confidence gained from the successful rural Saemaul Undong, which started in rural areas with the Saemaul spirit, we expanded it to factories and urban areas.
Thus, despite facing difficulties such as a shrinking and slowing global economy amidst the resource fluctuation crises of oil and food in 1973, we successfully overcame these trials and continued to achieve sustained growth.
Industrialization progressed further, and urbanization accelerated. Our aggregate national product increased remarkably. With the Saemaul spirit of diligence, self-help, and cooperation, the lives of all citizens were elevated and improved, and the comprehensive development of the national economy brought about a revolution in public life. This was indeed a Korean-style industrial revolution movement, serving as the starting signal for the modernization of the homeland by initiating and achieving in our generation the industrial revolution that our ancestors could not accomplish.
We finally encountered the opportunity to mark a new epoch in the history of a modern state on the foundation of the national economy.

### 3. A Precursor Movement for Establishing a Substantive Foundation for Democratization

The substantive realization of democracy requires a high level of economic growth and stability, as well as a high political and intellectual standard among the citizenry. Without these, merely imitating formats and institutions will result in nothing more than a hollow democracy. We must not forget that the maturity of British democracy today is built upon a firm economic foundation established through their industrialization.
Only with economic growth and stability can the political consciousness of citizens become rational, and their political behavior foster compromise and harmony.
The historical fact that France's long-standing political and social instability stemmed from hastily rushing political development without a foundation of economic growth or stability serves as a highly valuable lesson for us.
The question of how to choose the priority between political democratization and economic industrialization
23:
is an issue that must be decided very wisely and carefully, taking into account the historical traditions and realistic conditions of the country.
Saemaul Undong is an industrialization movement designed to pursue our economic development efficiently, systematically, and at an accelerated pace. We believe that we can gradually establish a political order of compromise, harmony, stability, and peace upon the economic foundation built through industrialization.
In other words, rather than repeating the vicious cycle of revolution caused by pursuing democratization prior to industrialization as in France, our ideal was to achieve economic development upon an economic foundation built through industrialization, and ultimately establish a peaceful transition of power and a stable political culture as in Great Britain.
Through extensive experience, we have learned the fact that political development is not a product of political manipulation, but rather a product of history—a consequence of economic, social, and cultural evolution. Such empirical facts must serve as invaluable lessons for future political development, as the long, two-thousand-year intellectual background of democracy and the path of Western democratic culture experienced during the two-hundred-year process of implementing democracy offer sufficient explanation.

## 4. Saemaul Undong as a Movement to Reduce Regional Disparities

The most pressing task we must resolve together is the economic issue. Within this economic framework, issues of production, distribution, and consumption must be incorporated.
No one can dispute that the outcomes of industrialization and manufacturing that we pursued since the 1960s brought remarkable growth in terms of aggregate Gross National Product (GNP). Consequently, it is true that our national power has strengthened, and the lives of individual citizens have become prosperous and elevated. In other words, we have all escaped absolute poverty. However, this did not mean that all of our economic issues were completely resolved.
In our pursuit of efficiency and speed in the process of economic growth, we discovered that unintended economic and social side effects were arising. This manifested as disparities, disconnections, and the resulting socio-cultural dual
24:
# restructuring problem.

Specifically, disparities across industries, social classes, and regions began to trigger serious social issues. Ideally, we should resolve these problems concurrently; however, this is impossible. This is because the human and material constraints required to address all these issues at once are too significant. Although we deeply recognize the imperative necessity that we must resolve these issues ourselves, the reason we cannot easily commit to attempting a simultaneous resolution lies precisely in our economic immaturity. However, the most fundamental issue requiring priority resolution was the regional disparity between urban and rural areas.

In the meantime, urbanization progressed rapidly through industrialization and manufacturing, leading farmers to concentrate in cities where economic incomes were higher and life was more comfortable. As a result, social problems were triggered in both urban and rural areas respectively. Income disparities emerged between urban and rural areas, which in turn led to differences in the quality of life. It was only natural that this created a sense of estrangement among the citizens. To narrow the gap between rural and urban areas and to elevate rural life to urban standards in both quality and scope, it was essential to modernize the countryside. This rural modernization movement manifested as the rural Saemaul Undong. We had to research strategies and techniques for rural modernization, which was none other than Saemaul Undong itself.

By paving roads, repairing roofs, building bridges, and fixing fences, Saemaul Undong successfully achieved significant improvements in the rural living environment. Through the course of this movement, farmers gained the conviction that they, too, could "live well" if they were diligent, self-reliant, and cooperative. Along with the self-confidence that "we too can prosper," a turning point for motivation was established. Consequently, they realized that through Saemaul Undong, their environment could be improved, their lives elevated, and culture enjoyed. All of us began to work more diligently, save more, and plan our lives systematically. In this sense, Saemaul Undong clearly served as a catalyst for a spiritual revolution, instilling courage and self-confidence in the farmers.

Although Saemaul Undong thus began as a movement to live well, it expanded and deepened over time to encompass the improvement of the living environment, the reform of consciousness, and the enhancement of household income, while gradually working to reduce regional disparities.

## 5. Saemaul Undong as a Multi-purpose Comprehensive Development Movement

Saemaul Undong was initiated with farmers as the main agents in rural areas to modernize the countryside and reduce disparities between urban and rural areas.
Historically, farmers possess a strong attachment to the land, as it serves as the foundation for their livelihood and production, and is the place where their ancestors' bones are buried. By forming ties of blood, geography, and spiritual connections centered on the land, they have maintained a community of life over a long period. From this, the simple love for one's hometown arises among the farmers, and patriotism and empathy sprout, which in turn becomes the farmers' nationalistic consciousness.
Beneath the surface of our national psyche, such a nationalistic consciousness flows continuously. This can be attributed to our geopolitical conditions as well as our historical experiences. It can be said that Saemaul Undong ignited precisely this underlying, deep-seated mindset of the farmers.
Without the foundation of local and national love possessed by the farmers, Saemaul Undong would have never expanded or deepened. Because it existed, Saemaul Undong was able to unleash an astonishing potential.
In the meantime, Saemaul Undong struck a chord with the citizens, and through the process of the movement, they maintained vast experience and firm conviction. Consequently, the flame spread to cities, factories, workplaces, and schools, and as a result, Saemaul Undong formed a consensus in our daily lives and production, both consciously and unconsciously.
Consequently, Saemaul Undong became the symbol of Korea's modernization in the 1970s and solidified as the foundation of national life. To that extent, Saemaul Undong penetrated deeply into our consciousness and daily lives, beginning to take root.
In our long history, there is no precedent where the entire nation united as one, dedicating its passion and solid cooperation, and focusing its utmost efforts on the modernization of the homeland and the construction of a wealthy and strong state
26:
to dedicate themselves in such a manner.
Such national cohesion and labor were not in vain; we achieved our long-cherished goal of 10 billion dollars in exports ahead of schedule, reached a per capita national income of 1,000 dollars ahead of time, and produced 41 million seok of rice, achieving self-sufficiency in our staple grain. It goes without saying that the spiritual foundation laid by Saemaul Undong provided significant support in achieving these target goals ahead of the scheduled years.
We have come to take proud pride in the fact that our generation, living today, has become a major driving force in the modernization of our homeland through Saemaul Undong.
Saemaul Undong expanded regardless of region, social class, workplace, age, or gender, and the Saemaul spirit spread to all spheres of citizens' lives, becoming the spiritual driving force for national development.
If the Saemaul Undong of the 1970s focused on improving the quality of public life through material production increases, the Saemaul Undong of the 1980s holds its significance as a spiritual revolution movement aimed at developing the qualitative aspects of citizens' lives. Thus, the movement's purpose lies in building a new society through the harmony of these two dimensions, enabling all of us to realize a fulfilling life.

### Section 3. The Korean Nation and Korean History

#### 1. The Origins of the Korean Nation

Regarding the origins of the Korean nation, there are generally two views: the southern origin theory and the northern origin theory.
As archaeological evidence for the southern origin theory, the single-edged stone adze is proposed, because this tool, used in various Southeast Asian islands and Polynesia, is also distributed across the Korean Peninsula via the Ryukyu Islands and Northern Kyushu. Additionally, tattooing and double-burial are cited as ethnological evidence. These are, of course, southern tools or customs. Nevertheless, their numbers are small, and such phenomena are found only south of the Han River. This is precisely where the limitations of the southern origin theory lie.
27:
# Chapter 1. Historical Background of Saemaul Undong

These difficulties of the southern origin theory ultimately strongly suggest that the Korean nation originated from the north. This is fully supported by both linguistic and archaeological evidence.

The Korean language belongs to the Buyeo and Proto-Han lineage branched from the northern Altaic languages and is said to share a genetic relationship with Altaic languages such as Turkish, Mongolian, and Tungusic. The Buyeo branch developed into the Goguryeo language, while the Han branch developed into the Silla and Baekje languages. Furthermore, a branch of the Buyeo language crossed the sea and formed the foundation of the Japanese language.

From this perspective, while the languages of the Three Kingdoms period shared a close relationship—particularly the Silla and Baekje languages—they cannot be said to have been identical. The unification of the language was triggered by the unification of the Three Kingdoms in the mid-7th century. From around this time, the Silla language of the Gyeongju region took center stage, absorbing the Baekje and Goguryeo languages, and developing into ancient Korean.

Not only is the linguistic lineage linked to the north, but prehistoric artifacts are also connected to the north.

Neolithic people, characterized by the use of stone tools and pottery, appeared on the Korean Peninsula around 4000 B.C. These earliest Neolithic people used plain pottery, which is thought to be lineage-linked to Siberia.

People using comb-patterned pottery, which is representative of the Neolithic Age, began to be active in various parts of the country around 3000 B.C.

The relationship between Bronze Age people (plain pottery users) and Neolithic people (comb-patterned pottery users) remains unclear. However, plain pottery sites and comb-patterned pottery sites are clearly distinguished, no matter how closely they are located. This fact suggests that the two groups lived under different conditions and likely differed ethnically.

The plain pottery users were not only armed with bronze weapons but were also capable of stable food supply through agriculture. Therefore, they are thought to have easily absorbed, assimilated, or slaughtered the comb-patterned pottery users, who were numerically inferior and still in the hunter-gatherer stage.

These Bronze Age people (plain pottery users) were likely the Dongyi (Eastern Barbarians), such as the Yemaek (or Ye and Maek) and Han, recorded in ancient Chinese texts, and the Neolithic people (comb-patterned pottery users) who were absorbed, assimilated, or
28:
expelled by them are assumed to be Paleo-Asiatics.
In short, the Korean nation reached its current form through a process where the Bronze Age people (plain pottery users, Dongyi) who migrated southward formed the mainstream by absorbing, assimilating, or expelling the Neolithic people (comb-patterned pottery users) and Paleo-Asiatics, with some southern elements added over time.

## 2. The Growth of the Korean Nation

After the Dongyi people entered Manchuria and the Korean Peninsula, they grew into a nation relatively smoothly. Without undergoing major migrations or significant intermarriage with other ethnic groups, they lived as a community bound by blood in the same region, sharing a relatively uniform culture.
However, a nation was not formed in prehistoric times; rather, it was established gradually alongside social development. In clan societies, they merely grew as tribes. Nonetheless, the countless clans that constituted tribes were the seeds for the future nation. Through the walled-town state period, which was the earliest form of statehood, clans began to merge. This was the heartbeat of nation-building.
Thus, numerous walled-town states merged into five or six confederated kingdoms, which in turn consolidated into Goguryeo, Baekje, and Silla. While these kingdoms competed for supremacy, the momentum for unification matured. Until this time, the stage of activity for the Dongyi was generally Manchuria and the Korean Peninsula south of the Liao River and Songhua River.
In the mid-7th century, the rivalry among the Three Kingdoms ended, and unification was achieved by Silla. This unification was, of course, incomplete. This was because the Manchurian region, which had been the active stage of the Three Kingdoms, was excluded from its territory, and Goguryeo refugees went on to establish Balhae there. Therefore, Silla's unification of the peninsula was actually limited to the area south of the Taedong River and the Wonsan Bay line.
Nevertheless, Silla's unification of the peninsula carried significant historical significance, primarily because it laid the foundation for the formation of the Korean nation on an independent basis. Although Unified Silla, along with Balhae, formed the Northern and Southern States period, and the two states opposed each other, Unified Silla's territory and population... and

the social, linguistic, and cultural foundations they established formed the mainstream of Korean history. In this respect, the unification of the Three Kingdoms by Silla holds immense national historical significance.

Silla was the last among the Three Kingdoms to establish an ancient state system. While Goguryeo began organizing its system around the 1st century A.D. and Baekje around the 3rd century A.D., Silla began its systemization only around the 3rd century A.D.

What, then, was the reason that Silla became the central agent of unification and subsequently formed the mainstream of Korean history? It is believed that this must be found in the fact that Silla preserved its indigenous culture for a long period. As is well known, Silla imported advanced culture the latest among the Three Kingdoms due to its geographical location. Consequently, the organization of its system as an ancient state was inevitably delayed. On the other hand, this had the advantage of allowing Silla to preserve its indigenous culture for a longer duration. It is believed that this tradition of indigenous culture fostered a strong spirit of independence and self-reliance among Silla's people, and further enabled the emergence of outstanding leaders, which ultimately led to the unification of the Three Kingdoms.

Following the fall of Balhae in the early 10th century and the rise of Goryeo to replace Silla, the northern recovery movement was actively pursued. Goryeo, by placating or conquering the Balhae people in the north, recovered most of Pyongan Province except for the Yalu River basin in the northwest, and the Hamgyong Province region up to Yeongheung in the northeast.

Goryeo's northern expansion policy was temporarily halted in the early 13th century with the powerful rise of the Mongol (Yuan) Empire. However, it was resumed during the Yuan-Ming transition period in the mid-14th century, recovering almost all of Pyongan Province and the Hamgyong Province region up to Gilju. Subsequently, aiming to advance into Manchuria, Goryeo attacked the Liaodong region twice.

The expansion of our territory to the Yalu and Tumen River lines occurred in the early 15th century. King Sejong, inheriting the undertakings left by Goryeo, established the Four Counties in the northwest (upper reaches of the Yalu River) and reclaimed the Six Garrisons in the northeast, securing the contemporary borders at the Yalu and Tumen River lines. Although the Four Counties were temporarily abandoned later, this did not signify the relinquishment of territory, and the Yalu River line in the northwestern region was continuously maintained.
30:
With the border solidified at the Yalu and Tumen River lines in the early 15th century, the northern expansion policy ceased. However, since the early 17th century, private migration to Manchuria and the Maritime Province began, and their numbers grew over generations, reaching approximately 2 million by the 1940s; these migrants were particularly concentrated in the Gando region. Consequently, a dispute over the sovereignty of Gando arose early on between Joseon and Qing, known as the Gando Issue. In this way, we can rediscover the territorial domain of the Korean nation.

### 3. The Development of National History

Through what stages has Korean society developed to reach its current state? In particular, how can the trajectory of Korean history be summarized when categorized by the social ruling class based on the status system?

This question should naturally be considered starting from the Paleolithic Age. However, since research and excavation of the Paleolithic period have only recently begun, its social aspects remain largely unknown; the outlines of society begin to take shape from the Neolithic Age.

The fundamental social unit of the Neolithic Age appears to have been the clan. Within the clan, families existed, and tribes composed of several clans were also formed. However, the most basic unit of social organization is believed to have been the clan.

This clan society operated under communal principles. Major clan matters were decided in clan councils, and they are thought to have engaged in collective production and distribution. Consequently, clan members maintained an equal relationship with one another, and even if a clan leader existed, they were merely an elected representative who could be removed at any time for misconduct.

Judging by these various characteristics of clan society, it is evident that no privileged status class was formed. That is to say, the entirety of the clan members were the owners, and all of them constituted the ruling power leading the clan society.

The formation of a ruling class began with the onset of the Bronze Age. What clearly illustrates this is the dolmen. A dolmen was a tomb built to bury a single individual.
31:
## Chapter 1 Historical Background of Saemaul Undong

Some were massive structures, topped with a coverstone measuring up to 9 meters in length and weighing 70 tons. Furthermore, these stones had been transported from places tens of li away. This suggests that the individual buried within, or the person who constructed it, was a ruling authority capable of mobilizing a significant number of people.

The newly emerged social ruling class maintained residences distinct from those of ordinary peasants. They lived in walled towns that were distinguished from common villages. These walled towns were situated within earthen fortifications constructed on low hills, and such earthen fortifications were distributed across various parts of the country.

These new ruling classes residing in the walled towns dominated the peasants who lived in villages and engaged in agriculture. It is believed that private land ownership among peasants had already emerged by this time. Consequently, a process of social differentiation likely occurred among the villagers, leading some to decline into hired laborers or slaves. Additionally, villagers appear to have cultivated communal village lands in addition to their private plots. Therefore, it is thought that a communal character was still maintained within village society.

These walled-town states later allied with one another to form larger states—confederated kingdoms. This period is estimated to be around the 4th century B.C., coinciding with the introduction of Bronze Age culture. However, even though confederated kingdoms were formed and thus kings existed, the actual ruling power is believed to have remained in the hands of the rulers of the individual walled-town states.

Thus, with the transition into the Bronze Age, a ruling class was established, and the peasantry differentiated into several social strata. This phenomenon can be considered a milestone change in the history of social development.

With the onset of the Three Kingdoms period, social patterns underwent another transformation. The ruling class at the center of society consisted of residents of the capital city, particularly the aristocracy, who were endowed with privileges under a rigid status system. The emergence of this central aristocracy allowed them to seize hegemony over politics, the economy, and culture.

In the case of Goguryeo, eligibility for the title of Gochuga was restricted to the royal family and the queen's clan. Similarly, in Baekje, the royal family and the queen's clan monopolized high ministerial offices, and in particular, the governorships of key regional strongpoints, such as the Damro, were exclusively held by the royal family. This fact indicates that in both states, a very narrow range of aristocratic families centered around the royal family formed the social ruling class.
32:
This aspect was even more evident in the case of Silla. Silla had eight status tiers, comprising Seonggol (sacred bone), Jingol (true bone), and six Dupum (head-rank) grades from the sixth head-rank down to the first head-rank. Among these eight status tiers, while Seonggol was undoubtedly dominant, it was the Jingol class that held hegemony over politics, the economy, the military, and society after the unification of the Three Kingdoms.
However, the families belonging to the Jingol class were extremely limited. First and foremost, the royal Kim clan formed the vast majority, followed by the queen's clan, the Park family. Their numbers do not seem to have been very large; although the lineage of Kim Gyeong-sin was also treated as Jingol, their presence was minor. Therefore, the core of Silla's ruling class was the royal Kim clan within the Jingol class.
However, as Silla entered its late period (the late 8th century), forces emerged to challenge the Jingol hegemony. One such development was the advancement of the sixth head-rank (Yukdupum) class. These individuals possessed academic intellect and Confucian refinement, and they were well-acquainted with the imperial civil service examination system of the Tang Dynasty, which recruited officials based on individual ability. Consequently, they criticized the Kolpum (bone-rank) system and demanded to be treated equally with the Jingol class.
Of even greater significance was the emergence of local clans (chwijok). Among these local clans were former Jingol or sixth head-rank elites who had returned to the countryside. However, many of them appear to have been village chiefs (chonju) who had grown as local forces from early on. Calling themselves castle lords (seongju) or commanders (janggwan), they exercised administrative, military, and economic control over specific regions. This ultimately undermined the power base of the Jingol aristocracy, a process further accelerated by peasant rebellions erupting in various regions. Consequently, these local clans replaced the Jingol and emerged as the practical social ruling class.
It was also due to the support of these local clans that Wang Geon, King Taejo of Goryeo, was able to unify the Later Three Kingdoms (in the early 10th century). Therefore, he had no choice but to adopt a policy of alliance with the local clans. However, as successive kings after Taejo pursued a strong policy of central government centralization, the local clans gradually lost their independent power and were either absorbed into the central aristocracy or saw their social status lowered to local officials (hyangri). In this manner, by the early 11th century (during the reign of King Hyeonjong), Goryeo society was transformed into a centralized aristocratic society.
This newly formed aristocratic society was one that respected social status based on lineage.
33:
Therefore, individual advancement was determined by social status rather than personal capability. Accordingly, marriage was in principle contracted among the aristocracy itself, and alliance with powerful families, particularly the royal family—the pinnacle of the aristocracy—was deemed most desirable.

The dominant force in this aristocratic society comprised the powerful families of Gyeonggi lineage residing in the capital, Gaegyeong. Excluding the Choi and Kim clans of Gyeongju, their ancestral seats (bongwan) are said to have been confined to the south of Jabiryong Pass, west of Daegwallyeong Pass, and north of the Sobaek Mountains.
In Goryeo aristocratic society, the civil aristocracy held precedence over the military aristocracy. The civil-military dual system (Yangban system) was introduced into the political system in the early Goryeo period, and families that produced civil officials were clearly distinguished from those producing military officials. Many military officials were of peasant origin, rising through the ranks of the military, and some were even of lowborn (cheonmin) status. Although individuals of local official (hyangri) origin sometimes became civil officials by passing the civil service examination, their original background was considered of local elite (hyangjok) status, which did not compromise the social dignity of the central civil aristocracy.
The Goryeo status system, centered on the civil aristocracy, was challenged by the military officials (Muban) who had not received proper treatment. In the late 12th century, the military officials finally overthrew the power of the civil aristocracy, the highest ruling class, and established a military regime. From then on, military officials were able to enjoy rights equal to those of civil officials.
Thus, while the Military Rebellion nominally elevated the status of military officials to a level similar to that of civil officials, it also severely destabilized the ruled classes. Peasants, who formed the foundation of society, launched movements to fundamentally alter the status system, and even among slaves, a powerful status liberation movement arose. As a result of these popular rebellions, the lowborn institutional districts (hyang, so, and bugok) that had persisted since the Silla period gradually disappeared.
Although local officials (hyangri) had avenues to advance to the civil bureaucracy through the civil service examination, they were excluded from the Jeonsigwa (land-grant system) regulations. This exclusion became even more pronounced as agricultural estates (農莊) expanded after the rise of the military regime. Consequently, the newly emerging scholar-officials (sadaebu) of local official origin found themselves in opposition to the central aristocracy and powerful families (gwonmun sejok). They strongly desired a restructuring of Goryeo society, and eventually allied with the military faction led by Yi Seong-gye to establish the Joseon Dynasty at the end of the 14th century, thereby emerging as the new ruling class.
34:
Once scholar-officials obtained public office, they belonged to the Yangban class, which comprised both civil (Munban) and military (Muban) officials. Consequently, the term Yangban gradually came to designate the social class eligible to hold civil and military offices. The general use of the title Yangban became widespread after the founding of the Joseon Dynasty. Therefore, the Joseon period, in which the Yangban status class constituted the ruling elite, can be referred to as a Yangban society.

The Yangban society, which had enjoyed privileged status, also underwent a process of decline after the 17th century, and discriminatory treatment against concubines' offspring (적서) began to ease. Yangban who had long been excluded from political power returned to the countryside, and some among them fell to the status of tenant farmers, leading to a process of dissolution within the Yangban society.

Conversely, the social advancement of the middle class (Jungin) became prominent. They expanded their horizons through travel abroad, accumulated wealth, and thereby elevated their social standing. Furthermore, through their specialized knowledge and administrative capabilities, they began to assert new claims for the rightful positions they deserved. They responded sensitively to Catholicism and enlightenment thought, and many ideological pioneers of the new era emerged from their ranks.

Peasants who lost their land declined into agricultural laborers, artisans, or mine workers, marking the emergence of a wage-laborer class. On the other hand, with the widespread adoption of the new rice transplanting method (이앙법), large-scale farming (광작) increased, and wholesale merchants (dogo) grew in urban areas. These large-scale farmers and wholesale merchants expanded their social influence on the strength of the wealth they had accumulated.

Meanwhile, slaves at the bottom of society were also gradually achieving liberation from their status. In the case of public slaves, the state eventually burned the slave registries (노비안), liberating them from lowborn status, and this phenomenon was increasingly observed in the case of private slaves as well. These various phenomena indicated that Yangban society was gradually transforming into a new form of society. In particular, the growth of the enlightenment faction (Gaehwapa) in urban areas and the Donghak movement in rural areas, both prominent from the late 19th century onward, played a decisive role in this trend. Consequently, the privileges enjoyed by the Yangban were stripped, Yangban society collapsed, and the obsolete status system vanished.

Thus far, the development process of Korean history has been examined, focusing on changes in the social ruling class. Up until the Unified Silla period (the end of the 9th century), which can be summarized by the bone-rank (Kolpum) system, society was one in which only the Jingol class

However, as it gradually transitioned into a ruling aristocratic society after the early 10th century, the scope of the social ruling class widened, and a certain degree of mobility between social strata began to occur. ### Section 4 Geopolitical Specificity of Korea

#### 1. Geopolitical Significance of the Territory

Geographical conditions exert the greatest influence on determining the destiny of a nation. This means that the quality and quantity of the national territory and population serve as critical factors in determining its destiny, as they constitute immutable security conditions.

However, national territory cannot be associated with security by examining it solely from a static perspective. Dynamic elements—namely, political relations among nations—must be integrated, and it must be understood geopolitically. For instance, if our territory were situated next to Chozhou, our national destiny would have unfolded in a vastly different direction than it did. Similarly, if our neighborhood were surrounded only by weak and small nations, our history would have taken a completely different course.

Therefore, it is necessary to comprehend this from a geopolitical perspective that combines static geography with dynamic political concepts. The central location and peripheral location can be considered key geopolitical characteristics that have exerted a major influence on our history. In this regard, this section will examine these two locations in relation to security and analyze the vulnerabilities of Korea from a lower-dimensional perspective of national defense geography. In doing so, we hope to understand some of the immutable challenges to our national security.
36:
## 2. Central Location and Security

The geopolitical characteristics of the Korean Peninsula that have exerted a major influence on our history can be broadly classified into two aspects: its central location and its peripheral location.
The concept of the Korean Peninsula's central location is understood to encompass the following two aspects:
① It occupies a central position surrounded by the four major powers: the United States, China, Japan, and the Soviet Union.
② It acts as a midway point between the continental advancement route of Japan (a maritime power) and the line of influence of continental powers (primarily China).
Of these two concepts of central location, the latter characteristic will be discussed when dealing with the peripheral location; thus, this section will analyze the peninsula solely from the perspective of its central location within the relations of the four major powers.
Excluding political elements and viewing it purely from a geographical standpoint, Korea is surrounded by the three major powers of China, Japan, and the Soviet Union.
However, until the eastward expansion of the Soviet Union (which was most actively pursued from the 1850s to the 1880s) and the modernization of Japan following its opening and the Meiji Restoration, the concept of a triangular central position could not be established; rather, it was merely conceived as a location appended to the Chinese continent.
When it was in a position appended to the continent, the destiny of the Korean Peninsula changed in accordance with transitions in China (the Central Plains). The rise of the Tang Dynasty coincided with its increased influence on Korea and the achievement of unification. The prosperity of the Yuan Dynasty was accompanied by its invasion of Goryeo, and the transition between the Ming and Qing Dynasties led to the birth of the Joseon Dynasty in Korea. The Joseon Dynasty continuously remained under Chinese influence.
However, following the eastward expansion of the Soviet Union and the opening of Japan, the influence on the Korean Peninsula shifted from a single line of influence from the Chinese continent to a three-way interaction. The power struggles over the Korean Peninsula in the 1880s illustrate this shift. In other words, when viewed as a relative concept, the late Joseon Dynasty entered a central position where its historical destiny was determined by the influences of these three nations.
Although it remained geographically situated at the center of the three powers after the Russo-Japanese War, the peninsula fell under the unilateral political influence of Japan as it came under Japanese rule.

After liberation, as the United States began to exercise political influence in this region, the peninsula came to be situated at the center of four major powers rather than three. Naturally, the relations among the four powers involving the United States after liberation shifted as follows:
① 1940s: A central position between the United States and the Soviet Union
② 1950s: A central position among the United States, China, and the Soviet Union
③ 1960s: A central position among the United States, China, the Soviet Union, and Japan
As illustrated above, due to the dynamics of power generated by the political influence of the four major powers, the central position has shifted from the center of two nations to three, and finally to four.
Generally, small nations surrounded by powerful states are susceptible to the following influences and destinies:

① Division and partition by major powers
② Dominance by one of the major powers or a coalition of states
③ Survival as a buffer zone or in a neutral position

Among the three possibilities mentioned above, surviving as a buffer (or neutral) zone is the norm; however, attempts frequently arise for one side to seize control of the small nation to maintain a favorable power balance. The Korean Peninsula served as a buffer zone until it fell under unilateral Japanese rule after Japan's victories in the wars against Qing China and Russia, and following liberation, it suffered the fate of partition.
Under the current state of division within this central position among the four powers, our destiny will undergo critical directional decisions in relation to the following three scenarios:
First, if the major powers adopt a stance of minimal intervention (a passive policy of disengagement), a 'showdown concept' may emerge between North and South Korea, raising the risk of war. Phenomena such as the withdrawal of U.S. forces serve as prime conditions for this scenario.
Other scenario is when the major powers pursue a buffer zone status quo (or neutralization) and agree on stabilization, the risk of war decreases, but resolving division—namely, achieving unification—becomes more difficult. Measures such as hollowizing (nullifying) the collective security systems that the United States, China, and the Soviet Union have respectively established with South or North Korea, or agreeing on the institutionalization of peace, or guaranteeing peace, can be viewed as neutralization; however, this implies freezing the status quo,

which can result in making unification difficult.
Given our position at the center of these major powers, we must consider several potential paths.
① We can seek national security through alliances with some of the major powers.
In this scenario, we can envision an alliance with the United States and cooperation with Japan, while it is natural for North Korea to form alliances with China and the Soviet Union.
② A method could be to independently check and balance the major powers against one another while securing our own security and capacity for unification.
This would involve establishing a self-reliant national defense posture, maintaining relative neutrality in relations with the four major powers, and choosing a politically and diplomatically focused policy direction.
③ A path of pursuing collective security with backing from major powers while simultaneously establishing a self-reliant defense posture.
This parallel policy direction is deemed even more necessary and inevitable for South Korea than for North Korea.

### 3. Peripheral Location and Security

The Korean Peninsula is currently considered to be in a peripheral position in several respects. Examples are as follows:
① Geographical Peripheral Zone: It is situated on the periphery of the ocean and the continent. Consequently, North and South Korea are respectively positioned at the frontiers of maritime and continental powers.
② Political Peripheral Zone: Situated at the frontiers of the free world and the communist world, North and South Korea nevertheless remain outside the core of global power politics. In terms of power, they still belong to the periphery of global politics.
③ Cultural Peripheral Zone: Global values did not originate from the Korean Peninsula; capitalist culture and communist culture, rooted in the West and Russia, have permeated South and North Korea, respectively. Thus, even culturally, the peninsula constitutes a peripheral zone rather than a core zone.
④ Economic Peripheral Zone: In terms of the economic distinction between advanced and developing nations, South and North Korea have failed to enter the core of economic power and are not yet included in the ranks of advanced nations,
39:
## Chapter 1 Historical Background of Saemaul Undong

making them a peripheral zone.

As described above, the Korean Peninsula belongs to the peripheral zone in various aspects, including politics, economy, culture, and geography. However, when viewed from a security perspective, its geographical peripherality must be emphasized. Therefore, this section will examine the characteristics of its geographical peripherality in greater detail. The theory of a geographical peripheral zone carrying military character derives from both the maritime-centric and continental-centric theories. Regardless of which theory is applied, the Korean Peninsula is clearly a peripheral zone. In other words, the Korean Peninsula belongs to the intermediate peripheral zone (Rimland) conceptualized by Nicholas J. Spykman.
Let us first examine the peripherality of the Korean Peninsula from the perspective of maritime-centric theory, as argued by Alfred Thayer Mahan.

He understood international politics as an ongoing struggle for command of the sea. It was not the land, but the oceans surrounding the land that drew his attention. He argued that because the sea serves as a transport route incomparably superior to land, nations that dominate maritime shipping routes become global powers.
Just as Britain's dominance over the seas collapsed Napoleon's continental system, major political and military decisions in history have been made by nations possessing command of the sea. This was because maritime powers enjoyed far superior transportation systems and mobility compared to continental powers.

Next, let us observe the peripherality of the Korean Peninsula from a continental-centric perspective.
Halford Mackinder is a representative proponent of continental-centric theory, and a unique feature of his theory is the heartland theory. It posits the existence of a core, or heartland, location on the continent. Around this continental heartland, continental power is formed, surrounded by peripheral regions, with insular (maritime) regions situated beyond them.
According to his theory, the nation that rules the heartland commands the continent and its peripheral zones, and thereby rules the world.

The heartland of Europe comprises Germany, France, and Austria, while the heartland of Asia is China. In this respect, the theory resembles Sinocentrism. The concept of the Central Plains (Jungwon) in Sinocentrism can be viewed in this light: the ruler who controls the Central Plains controls the surrounding
40:
periphery and thus rules 'all under heaven' (the world).
Whether viewed through Sinocentrism or the continental-centric theory that emphasizes the heartland, the Korean Peninsula is clearly a peripheral or frontier region, and this is especially true for South Korea. The peninsula is contiguous by land to the Chinese continent—the heartland of Asia—and is in contact with the Soviet Union's eastern outlet.
Due to its position on the periphery of the continent, South Korea experiences compounded security pressure from North Korea, which is backed by China and the Soviet Union. Even when Korea existed as a unified nation-state, it received considerable pressure from the power of the massive continent; however, following division, South Korea has effectively become a 'semi-peninsula,' thereby facing an even greater threat.
Under these geographical conditions, our strength to counter pressure (threats) from the north must remain superior.
South Korea is situated at the frontier of the maritime sphere of influence while simultaneously having to confront the frontier of continental powers. Consequently, South Korea's policies bear a dual nature: it must pursue a maritime-centric policy of cooperation with maritime nations, while simultaneously implementing a defense policy to guard against overland invasions. Because this dual policy contains inherent contradictions, it must be executed in harmony.

## 4. Characteristics of National Defense Geography

When examining Korean geography from the narrower perspective of national defense, several characteristic features can be identified.
First, it is a rectangular peninsular nation bordering China and the Soviet Union by land.
The Korean Peninsula extends across 10 degrees of latitude from 33 to 43 degrees North and lies between 124 and 131 degrees East longitude, exhibiting a territory configuration that is narrow east-to-west and long north-to-south.
To the north, a peninsula contiguous with China and the Soviet Union is formed.
However, South Korea forms a square peninsular shape extending between 33 and 38 degrees latitude, resulting in an extremely narrow territory.
Due to this territorial configuration, we are understood to experience the following impacts in terms of national defense.

① First, while North Korea is situated in a position to receive immediate support from China or the Soviet Union, South Korea requires a considerable amount of time to receive support from Japan, not to mention the United States, and also faces challenges in the deployment of such support. Consequently, South Korea faces the difficulty of having to secure supporting forces locally (through stationing).
② Second, due to its narrow land area, South Korea possesses vulnerabilities to attacks by modern equipment. Even if an airstrike is launched from any airbase located within North Korea, modern fighter-bombers can reach and strike South Korean territory within tens of minutes. In other words, because the depth of air operations is short, the nation possesses geographical conditions where severe damage can be inflicted before response measures can be implemented. Not only the depth of air operations but also the depth of land operations is short, meaning that the capital metropolitan area—a core region of South Korea—is vulnerable to not only rocket artillery but also long-range artillery attacks from the vicinity of the truce line.
③ Third, because South Korea is a peninsula, maritime connectivity supports its defense, but it also carries the risk of suffering significant damage from maritime infiltration and attacks. Unlike North Korea, South Korea, surrounded by the sea on three sides, enjoys advantageous defensive conditions provided by the sea. However, because its major cities (primarily industrial cities) are situated along the coast, there are concerns about substantial damage from maritime attacks. Furthermore, on the West Sea, the extreme tidal range and the presence of numerous islands make it difficult to detect infiltrating enemy spy boats via radar, representing a defensive vulnerability in certain aspects.

Second, the capital metropolitan area, including Seoul, is situated in close proximity to the truce line and falls within the range of the enemy's ground artillery. The targets of military attacks are customarily designated as military installations, industrial zones, and cities. Because cities contain both industrial and military facilities, major cities become prime targets of attack. South Korea's capital metropolitan area, which encompasses Seoul and its surrounding cities such as Incheon, Bucheon, Anyang, Seongnam, and Uijeongbu, is a critical region in several respects.
First, it is one of the key industrial zones. Among the industrial zones in South Korea, this

capital metropolitan area zone is critical. Thus, the gross production of the capital metropolitan area is approximately double that of North Korea's total gross production. Second, in terms of population, the population of the capital metropolitan area is equivalent to half of North Korea's total population. This represents more than a quarter of South Korea's population. As such, the capital metropolitan area occupies a central position of the nation not only economically but also in terms of politics, history, and culture.

From this perspective, it can be argued that the power that controls the capital metropolitan area is in a position to lead the nation, as this region accounts for nearly one-third of the total national capacity.

However, the capital metropolitan area is located a mere 40 km from the truce line. Thus, the capital metropolitan area, where population and assets are highly concentrated, is vulnerable to attacks by new long-range artillery, and fighter aircraft taking off from near the truce line can reach it within minutes.

Consequently, North Korea may be psychologically motivated to seize the capital metropolitan area in order to dominate the nation, while South Korea has no choice but to adopt a strategic concept of defending it to the death. One can imagine what kind of defense posture the United States would maintain if its capital were within the range of ground artillery and its neighboring nation possessed aggressive tendencies. In terms of national defense geography, this point must be regarded as our most critical vulnerability.

## 5. Issues Arising from These Characteristics

Looking at how South Korea's geopolitical characteristics pose problems for national security, we can observe vulnerabilities in several aspects:

1. Being located at the center of major powers, South Korea constantly faces the risk of invasion by them.
2. Located at the periphery of both maritime and continental spheres, it is positioned on the frontline of conflict.
3. Despite its peninsular status, South Korea, being divided, must bear defense disadvantages.
4. While North Korea shares borders with its supporting powers, South Korea is far removed from its key ally, the United States, placing it at a severe disadvantage in terms of receiving support.
5. With its capital metropolitan area within range of ground artillery, prioritizing national security is inevitable for South Korea.

## Section 6. Social Movements Prior to Saemaul Undong

### 1. The Mythological Meaning Embedded in Traditional Customs

While Saemaul Undong is defined as a movement to live well, this is not a unique concept that refers exclusively to Saemaul Undong.
Looking back at history, the desire to live well has always been intense since ancient times, and traces of efforts reflecting the socio-temporal characteristics of each era in which our ancestors lived are clearly evident in their search for ways to improve their lives.
In other words, as long as humans possess life, they are bound to harbor desires. As long as those desires coexist with life, the pursuit of methods for their satisfaction is of a nature that cannot be abandoned under any circumstances.
When examining chronologically what kind of movements were adopted, the naming and methods were not always identical, yet one unchanging commonality remains: the core meaning of satisfying the desire to live a better life remained constant.
From this perspective, we discover a self-evident logic: Saemaul Undong, chosen by us today, must also be understood through two distinct aspects—namely, the variable aspect and the invariable aspect.
The variable aspect refers to the name under which, and the methods and scale by which, the movement is deployed. The invariable aspect is that the essential nature of the movement to live well remains unchanged, regardless of modifications to its methods or scale.
In other words, while the methods oriented toward satisfying desires may change, the desires themselves do not undergo any fundamental alteration.

Although the development methods of various social movements prior to Saemaul Undong differed across eras, the fundamental nature of the desire to achieve a better life has remained entirely unchanged.

While the specific content of the desires pursued may have varied, the ultimate value sought never deviated from the central focus of achieving a better life.

A clear empirical example of this is "Gosine" (고시내), a folk custom that has been passed down through our nation's five-thousand-year history.
"Gosine" is also written as "Gosilnae" (고실내) or "Gosilrae" (고실래), but all of these terms consistently refer to Gosil-ssi.

According to *Gyuwon Sahwa* (규원사화), a text attributed to the author Bugae (북애), Gosil-ssi "first invented the fire-cooking agricultural method and taught the people how to sow and harvest." In addition, *Haedong Jukji* (해동죽지) by Choe Yeong-nyeon (최영년) explains that the practice of farmers taking a spoonful of rice and shouting "Gosine" before eating in the fields is a prayer for the descent and blessings of Gosil-ssi, the deity of agriculture (meaning: "Even if every household forgets the grace of feeding, they must shout 'Gosilrae' at every meal").

Whether or not the custom of Gosine originated from the historical figure of Gosil-ssi, it is clear that its persistence in our daily customs to this day represents a prayer and aspiration to live with abundance and be free from hunger.

In other words, "Gosine" is an expression of the fundamental human desire to achieve a better life.

Accordingly, this study traces chronologically the methods employed throughout history to realize this desire for a better life.
