### 3. Social Movements through Hyangyak
Compared to the Dure, Hyangyak (village covenant) was characterized by its operation at the township (myeon) level of the local community. However, unlike the Dure, it did not involve the direct participation of all members of the local community. It was based on the principle of voluntary participation, and during that era of strict class divisions between the nobility (yangban) and commoners (sangmin), it was true that social class restrictions also applied to who could join the covenant.
Nonetheless, in all cases, Hyangyak carried a strong connotation of social education, utilizing practical virtues as a daily code of conduct. This can be easily inferred from the fact that its fundamental philosophy lay in "Hwamin Seongsok" (화민성속)—meaning to edify the populace and establish wholesome customs (wholesome customs and manners).
To achieve this philosophy, four major pillars have been proclaimed as the primary practical virtues: 1) Encouraging virtue (Deogeop Sangwon), 2) Correcting errors (Gwasil Sanggyu), 3) Associating with propriety (Yesok Sanggyo), and 4) Assisting each other in times of hardship and disaster (Hwannan Sanghyul). (Although the phrasing of these virtues may vary slightly depending on the case, their meanings all align with these four virtues.)
Hyangyak is said to have originated with the four Lu brothers who lived in the Landian region of Song Dynasty, China. The Lu Hyangyak (Yeossi Hyangyak) was supplemented by Zhu Xi (Jumungong) and was introduced to Korea as the Yean Hyangyak of Yi Hwang in 1556.
Even before Yi Hwang's Yean Hyangyak, there was the Pungpae Hyangyak established by King Taejo Yi Seong-gye in 1398. The Pungpae Hyangyak can be considered the pioneer of Hyangyak in Korea. It consisted of 41 articles that prescribed negative obligations (prohibitions), and thus was also referred to as the 41 Articles of Hyangyak
54:
.

Subsequently, it was expanded by Prince Hyoryeong to include 21 virtuous items and 35 evil items, totaling 56 articles, and was therefore also referred to as the 56 Articles of Hyangyak.

The Pyeongyang Hyangyak was created for implementation in the Hamheung region, the birthplace of Yi Seong-gye (Taejo). It was named Pyeongyang Hyangyak because Yi Seong-gye chose to name it after the birthplace of Emperor Gaozu of Han in China, rather than calling it Hamheung Hyangyak.

On the other hand, the covenant named after its actual implementation region, the Yean Hyangyak by Yi Hwang, consisted of 28 articles. Its content carried a strong intent to purify social customs, and it represents a type of covenant that pursued creation through imitation.

Notably, Yi I went a step further, establishing and implementing the Paju Hyangyak in 1560, the Seowon Hyangyak in 1571, and the Haeju Hyangyak in 1579 within their respective local communities.

Yi I clearly stated in the Paju Hyangyak that, regardless of the era, all Hyangyak are based on the principles of: 1) being rooted in common human sentiments, 2) obeying the laws of nature, 3) purifying customs, 4) focusing on public edification, and 5) not violating propriety.

Furthermore, Yi I summarized the objectives of the Paju Hyangyak into two main points. First, to properly teach propriety to the villagers so that everyone returns to benevolence and righteousness (Gyoryeuii Gwiujeong). Second, to have leaders discuss all village affairs (common interests) with the residents and handle them with fairness and justice, thereby ensuring that the public interest and justice of the village remain robust (Simujung Ibokugo).

Moreover, Yi I indicated that while Hyangyak is a resident autonomy covenant movement implemented in rural villages, it ultimately aims to secure the stability of the people's livelihood—the foundation of the state—by establishing social discipline and eradicating mutual distrust among residents.

In other words, since a state cannot exist soundly if trust between the government and the people is lacking, Yi I clarified that the implementation of Hyangyak is intended to solidify the foundation of the livelihood of the people (Minmusin Bullip, Ibyak Soirip Minji).

Based on these fundamental principles, the Seowon Hyangyak (Neungcheon) not only materialized the systems for resident education and resident

organization methods. Meanwhile, the Haeju Hyangyak significantly incorporated economic elements in addition to cultural and moral values, developing distinctive content that aimed to promote moral influence on the foundation of a stable economic life.

Furthermore, Yi I created various social movement models to guide cooperative activities of residents, such as the Haeju Ilhyangyak, Sagye, and Pungsugye.

This tradition of social movements was succeeded by Silhak (Practical Learning) scholars such as Yu Gye and Jeong Sul. By the time of Ahn Jeong-bok (1712–1791), it evolved into the Hyangsabeop (rural community covenant), developing content that truly embodied the spirit of self-reliance.

First, in terms of organization, Ahn Jeong-bok's Hyangsabeop classified leadership figures into Tongsu, Gapjang, Sajeong, and Hyangsa (based on the organizational hierarchy: five households make a Tong, two Tong make a Gap, ten Gap make a Sa, and gathered Sa make a Hyang), establishing a four-level standard for resident organization.

Second, in terms of local governance, its content included: 1) warning each other against fire, 2) resisting thieves collectively, 3) assisting each other during disasters, 4) helping each other build housing, 5) respecting laws, and 6) assisting and respecting one another.

Third, in terms of education, it aimed to cultivate wholesome customs and manners through: 1) filial piety and obedience to parents, 2) respect for elders, 3) harmony among neighbors, 4) instruction of descendants, 5) stabilizing and promoting livelihood, and 6) avoiding deceitful behavior.

Fourth, regarding the promotion of propriety and customs, it placed great emphasis on all residents learning martial arts.

On the 1st and 15th of every month, residents were trained in archery at designated archery ranges (Sapo). This served as a national training plan to prepare for emergencies.

It was based on the principle of "Nonghan Seopsa"—engaging in livelihood during peacetime and mobilizing for defense training during the agricultural off-season.

In addition, as part of a plan to equip the local community with self-defense capabilities, each household and village was required to maintain a certain scale of defensive tools and weapons.

To enable residents to defend themselves using their own organization in times of emergency (such as invasions by foreign adversaries or bandits), the martial arts training and related etiquette were formalized as Hyangrye (local rituals), requiring the participation of all residents.

Fifth, in terms of economic guidance, efforts were made to educate and guide residents in their production activities, and to select and distribute crops suitable for the local soil.

Furthermore, it contained a significant amount of social purification content aimed at correcting corrupt customs such as social deviance, gambling, high-interest lending, dissipation, and luxurious
56:
waste.
Through these developmental pathways, Hyangyak fostered collective efforts by teaching residents that they must take responsibility for local development and seek self-reliance. It also placed great emphasis on cultivating the spirit and capability of self-defense—the idea that foreign aggression must be countered primarily through the united strength of the residents. In particular, the prominent self-defense characteristics found in local activities guided by Silhak scholars reflect a resolve never again to suffer the humiliation brought by the trials of war, such as the Imjin War and the Byeongja Horan.
Although Hyangyak began as a civilian-led local resident movement at the village level, its lineage was preserved. It persisted not only throughout the Joseon dynasty but was also practiced in some regions during the Japanese colonial rule under the name of Hyangdo Hyangyak.

### 4. Social Movements Prior to Liberation

Social movements in Korea under Japanese colonial rule can be broadly categorized into three types.
First, popular movements with anti-Japanese orientations aimed at reclaiming the nation.
Second, resident movements carrying the character of the Japanese assimilation education policy.
Third, self-reliance movements that aimed to preserve traditions and revitalize the national spirit without provoking the colonial authorities.
Reflecting on these types, the first struggled to achieve structured social organization, while the second could not clearly establish national identity or independent development systems. The third type, however, although outwardly accepting the assimilationist educational framework, possessed the potential to maintain and develop national traditions and local community characteristics under the banner of self-reliance.
From this perspective, this section focuses on the third type to examine the patterns of social movements prior to liberation.
It is a well-known fact that the assimilation policy of the Japanese regime, from the perspective of social

## 5. Community Movements after the Korean War

From the founding of the nation until the Korean War ended with an armistice, Korean society was in such a state of flux that this period could be described as an era of non-existent community movements.
For a nation that suffered over one million casualties and approximately three billion dollars in property damage during the war, finding a path to national self-reliance was one of the most urgent tasks. Consequently, a resident self-reliance movement from the perspective of developing community development projects was demanded.
Thus, the initiation of community development projects is believed to have begun in 1953, when the Korean government, in cooperation with the United Nations Korean Reconstruction Agency (UNKRA), formulated a two-year plan for community development.
Although it is recorded that 400 projects were completed under this plan, they were merely small-scale initiatives.
However, the organization of the Joint Korea-US Community Development Working Group by the Korea-US Joint Economic Committee on June 21, 1957, to review "whether community development projects could be implemented in Korea," can be regarded in a sense as the birth of community movements in Korea.
At that time, from the Korean side, the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, the Ministry of Health and Social Affairs, the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Home Affairs, and the Ministry of Reconstruction participated, while the Office of the Economic Coordinator (OEC) in Korea appointed representatives from the Community Development Division and related sectors. A joint survey team was formed from both sides to divide the Gwangju-gun area of Gyeonggi-do into four
60:
unit areas, and selected two villages from each unit area. In order to determine the feasibility, direction, and timing of the community development projects, a comprehensive social survey was conducted covering industry, education, communication, medical facilities, religion, and other aspects, which led to a promising conclusion.

The conclusions were: 1) Korean farmers are capable of improving their villages through their own efforts. 2) The modernization and development of Korean rural society require a certain level of external material support, introduction, and guidance.
Based on these conclusions, the working group recommended to the Korea-US Joint Economic Committee that community development projects in Korea should be implemented as demonstration projects with OEC assistance, incorporating both assisted and non-assisted initiatives, after which the working group was disbanded.
Subsequently, the Community Development Subcommittee within the Korea-US Joint Economic Committee was established as a new organization.
This subcommittee was tasked with: 1) selecting model villages for community development, 2) preparing for the Korea-US Community Development Conference, 3) appointing staff to the Central Community Development Committee, 4) preparing for staff training at the New Life Training Center, and 5) contracting technical assistance services with the American Korean Foundation.
Meanwhile, on January 24, 1958, the Korean government resolved the Guidelines for Community Development Projects at a cabinet meeting. To summarize the guidelines: First, community development was defined as "a process of social improvement activity in which residents within a certain area identify and resolve collective or individual difficulties for a better life, establish collective or individual plans, and execute them through their own efforts or with services and materials supplied from external sources (government or other institutions)."
Second, expenditures were to be covered by foreign aid supplies and counterpart funds.
Third, the demonstration plan was to be implemented in four areas, including Jeju-do.
Fourth, a consultative body was to be established under the Ministry of Reconstruction by Presidential Decree, with the Minister of Reconstruction serving as the chairman, and the vice-ministers of Home Affairs, Education, Agriculture and Forestry, Health and Social Affairs, and Reconstruction serving as committee members. Provincial and county committees were to be formed, with provincial governors and county magistrates serving as chairmen, to consult on projects alongside members appointed by the chairmen.

However, it is a fact that the 6-Year Self-Help Development Plan for Villagers faced various issues because it was fundamentally based on a balanced development model that sought to develop all 33,100 villages nationwide simultaneously.
In developing underdeveloped societies, general problems noted include ① lack of capital, ② lack of technology, ③ low educational levels, ④ lack of motivation, and ⑤ religious conventions, but achieving balanced development is particularly challenging in the field of community development.
Furthermore, under conditions where it is inherently difficult to systematically mobilize administrative leadership, it is extremely difficult to achieve significant outcomes.
Although it is customary to adopt the principle of unbalanced development strategy to overcome such difficulties in implementing development projects, the 6-Year Self-Help Development Plan for Villagers failed to deeply consider fundamental solutions to these problems. Consequently, it could not be revitalized and was likely sidelined as nothing more than a plan on paper.

### 6. Reconstruction National Movement

The National Movement (Act No. 1523, December 16, 1963), which began on December 17, 1961, was launched after the Act on the National Reconstruction Movement (enacted and promulgated under Act No. 622) was repealed and renamed the National Movement.
However, since the National Movement originated from the National Reconstruction Movement, the heading is presented as the National Reconstruction Movement here for convenience.
The National Movement was defined as "a movement in which the entire nation cooperates and unites under democratic ideals to build a welfare state, develops their hometowns with a spirit of self-reliance and self-help, and establishes a new lifestyle system."
To realize these movement ideologies, a systematic organizational structure was
64:
established. It maintained headquarters at the center, special branches and provincial branches in cities and provinces, and branch offices in cities, counties, and districts, with corresponding committees set up at each level.

Additionally, town, township, and village (Eup, Myeon, Ri, Dong) committees were set up at local levels to manage activities and projects related to the National Movement.

Furthermore, youth associations and women's associations were established to execute the projects of the National Movement under the direction and supervision of the village committees.

The primary indicators for the projects of the National Movement were presented as: ① cultivating national ideology, ② demonstrating fellowship among compatriots, ③ international cooperation, ④ hometown development, ⑤ livelihood improvement, ⑥ promoting a healthy social atmosphere, ⑦ local education, ⑧ guidance and cultivation of youth and women, and ⑨ other projects deemed necessary.

As a resolution to implement these ideological indicators of the National Movement, all staff, including the director, made a vigorous start based on an oath taken upon their inauguration: "We take pride in being servants of the entire nation, the cradle of national unity for the National Movement, and the leading force for hometown development."

The performance of activities and projects achieved through the National Movement was indeed substantial across various fields, but the defining characteristic of the movement's essence was its heavy emphasis on cultural activities.

In other words, because it did not place significant weight on production activities directly linked to the economic livelihood of residents, it seems to have struggled to take deep root in the daily lives of the general public.

Looking at the various types of social movements prior to Saemaul Undong, the community development movement right after the war could not settle even within the administrative framework due to systemic deficiencies in its promotional organization. Consequently, the Bureau of Community Development suffered from instability, shifting from the Ministry of Reconstruction to the Ministry of Construction, from the Ministry of Construction to the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, and further to the Rural Development Administration.

Similarly, the 6-Year Self-Help Development Plan for Villagers (1966–1971) formulated by the Rural Development Administration also failed to gain momentum due to its balanced, all-encompassing development approach.

Another point to note is that while the National Movement began in 1963 and the 6-Year Self-Help Development Plan for Villagers began in 1966, Saemaul Undong

began in 1970. This resulted in three movements with similar contents and characteristics overlapping with the launch of Saemaul Undong in 1970.
Consequently, general questions arose regarding the necessity of maintaining movements with similar contents, and it is a fact that this raised concerns about potential difficulties in preventing public confusion in perception and securing the integration of social forces.
Thus, the "National Movement Organization" was disbanded in the mid-1970s, and the "Villagers' Self-Help Improvement Movement" was absorbed into Saemaul Undong through the 6-Year Plan.
From this perspective, tracing the historical context of social movements in Korea reveals the prehistory leading up to Saemaul Undong, showing clearly that the core principles running through this prehistory directly connect to Saemaul Undong.
In other words, although the name Saemaul Undong was coined in the 1970s, the blood flowing through its systemic constitution was the same blood that has run through our nation's history.
This highlights the historical dimension of Saemaul Undong. By compensating for the shortcomings of prior movements, Saemaul Undong was structured as a newer and more advanced model of the "Better Life Movement" designed to realize our aspirations in the context of modern society.

## Section 7. The Launch of Saemaul Undong

### 1. Launching from Self-Awareness

The 1960s can be regarded as the preparatory stage for the launch of Saemaul Undong. During this decade, measures were introduced to wash away thousands of years of stagnation, liberate farmers from exorbitant usurious loans that blocked rural development, and guarantee agricultural product prices. In addition, rural modernization projects in the 1960s can be categorized into several aspects:
First, establishing a professional outlook and a sense of national identity among rural residents. At that time,
66:
rural residents, who accounted for 60% of the total population, did not settle in their occupations and, consequently, failed to secure their status as citizens. The dominant view at the time was that state reform must begin with rural reform and a mental revolution of rural residents. Because the majority of the population, the rural residents, did not focus on production, dependency on foreign food and raw materials increased. As a result, rural areas repeated a vicious cycle of poverty, which hindered Korea's economic and social development. Therefore, the goal was set that self-development and rural development for rural residents was indeed self-defense and national power reinforcement, which was one of the highest national policies at the time.

Second, the foundation for agricultural modernization was established, and rural administration was reformed. Water resources were developed to initiate all-weather farming, land consolidation was implemented to prepare for future agricultural mechanization, and the Rural Development Administration was reorganized to systematize agricultural technology guidance.

Third, the development of rural resources can be cited. Although rural resources do not refer solely to physical resources, the fact that self-sufficiency in major staple crops has been achieved today, import substitution for some raw materials has occurred, and we were able to withstand the global food crisis of 1973 is largely due to the agricultural development foundations laid in the 1960s.

Fourth, bold investment was made in rural areas. To boost the production motivation of rural residents and develop rural communities, massive funds and subsidies have been invested since the 1960s to solidify the foundation of development. Given that approximately 700,000 of the rural population were unemployed in 1962, the number of underemployed or potentially unemployed individuals must have been even higher.

Following the May 16 military coup, the Chairman of the Supreme Council for National Reconstruction, Park Chung-hee, wrote in 'The Nation, the Revolution, and I' that "the sun rising in Korea must rise not from the East Sea, but from the mountains and fields of our rural villages. For this is where our hope dawns." This illustrates how closely the rural areas of the 1960s were associated with the nation's future. In other words, this was a period when the potential of rural modernization had a profound impact on the development of the entire nation, not just on the countryside itself.

In this context, the launch of 'Saemaul Undong' was proposed as a movement to develop rural areas and awaken rural residents from the slumber of traditional society, encouraging them to join the ranks of national modernization. In effect, Saemaul Undong was born after a gestation period of approximately ten years.

Another motivation for the birth of Saemaul Undong was external stimuli. Den-

mark, New Zealand, Israel, and Japan, which were more advanced than Korea, mostly achieved their current developed status by starting with rural development. New Zealand since the 1850s and Israel since the early 1900s have systematically and plannedly developed their agriculture and rural areas. New Zealand, in particular, artificially developed its mountains and fields to suit agriculture, maintaining a per capita national income level of $7,000 since 1972. Furthermore, Korea was highly stimulated by the rapid development of countries that were colonies before World War II, such as the Philippines, Indonesia, and Thailand, which established the conditions for development by the mid-1950s. Although they are now far behind Korea, until around 1970, Thailand was ahead of us in income and development projects.

Under these domestic and international circumstances, Korea was destined to remain dependent on aid or stay a weak nation unless it effectively utilized its human resources to develop the national territory, honed technologies, and developed its scarce domestic resources. At this time, the unanimous aspiration of the people was how Korea could escape the yoke of being an underdeveloped or backward nation, win the inter-Korean confrontation, replace import-dominated markets with domestic products, and boost self-respect and pride as citizens of an independent nation.

It was at this critical juncture that Saemaul Undong began to sweep across rural areas, and in less than ten years, Korea reached the level of a newly industrializing country. The achievements of Saemaul Undong today were built upon the blood, sweat, and tears of the entire nation. For example, in 1971, the total value of Saemaul projects was calculated at 12.2 billion won, of which government support accounted for only 4.1 billion won, meaning that rural residents generated more than three times the government's support. In 1972, out of a total project performance of 31.3 billion won, residents' labor investment accounted for 21.1 billion won, representing 67% of the total performance.

In 1962, the farm household income per household was 62,000 won, but by 1979, it exceeded 2 million won, and per capita national income, converted to US dollars, was reportedly $81 in 1960. Although prices and currency values cannot be directly compared, it is an undeniable fact that we were at the level of an underdeveloped nation socially and economically compared to the present. There was a prevailing concern that at this level, our stance in the confrontation with North Korea would remain insecure. This was the predominant si-

tuation. North Korea had launched the Chollima Movement in the 1950s, later changing it to the Three Revolutions Movement, unifying the public spirit around production-oriented concepts and executing development projects, such that their per capita income exceeded ours until the 1960s.
Around this time, Korea was socially experiencing a strong urban-bound migration trend in rural areas, while egoism and decadent trends were prevalent in cities, and the socio-economic gap between urban and rural areas was widening. In short, it was a precarious state lacking shared social values.
Although some of these weaknesses were alleviated during the implementation of the 5-Year Economic Development Plan starting in 1962, there was no clear goal to establish a sense of self-reliance. It was at this moment that Saemaul Undong, aimed at rural revitalization, was presented. Looking back at this juncture, the proposal of Saemaul Undong was indeed an exceptionally fortunate development.

## 2. Practical Enactment of the Resolution for Modernization
On April 22, 1970, at the National Conference of Provincial Governors, it was resolved to study measures to stimulate rural self-help efforts based on cooperation among farmers, related agencies, and guidance personnel in accordance with government policy. Subsequently, on May 6 of the same year, guidelines for national land conservation were established, pledging to care for the national territory diligently and emphasizing the promotion of Saemaul Undong. With this, Saemaul Undong officially began. As mentioned previously, the reason Saemaul Undong had to start in rural areas first was that agriculture, in which the majority of the population was engaged, accounted for a high proportion of the national economy and was the key industry at the time.
In terms of internal reasons for starting in rural areas, the primary need was to re-establish values that would serve as the spiritual pillar for rural residents, and to mobilize the latent manpower in many rural villages for social and economic production to transform idle labor into productive force. In other words, the goal was to inspire a mental revolution among rural residents scattered by small-scale individual farming, to reform outdated traditional social lives through cooperation, to modernize production processes by injecting capital and technology, and to improve living environments and production conditions, leading to the so-

# Chapter 1. Historical Background of Saemaul Undong

called community development driven by the public.

At the start of Saemaul Undong, there was considerable discussion regarding the purity of its objectives and the conditions for its success or failure. Concerns arose as to whether it could develop into a truly innovative rural development movement given the conditions at the time, alongside apprehensions that the movement might be politically exploited. Although there were some trial and errors along the way, these concerns did not manifest significantly, and Saemaul Undong proceeded steadily.

The launching project of Saemaul Undong was environmental improvement in rural areas. The government provided 335 bags of cement to each village (Ri and Dong) and encouraged the rural residents to utilize idle labor during the farming off-season to attempt environmental improvement projects, known as 'Saemaul Beautification' (Saemaul Gakkugi).

The objective of the Saemaul Beautification project was to test the spiritual cooperation of the residents and to upgrade their housing environments.

This pilot project achieved remarkable results, with a cumulative total of 7.2 million people participating in the project in 1971. The residents themselves were the most surprised by the outcomes achieved through this pilot project. They derived the principle that self-reliance is possible through cooperation. The fact that regional development projects in Indonesia also provide a set amount of funding to villages to induce self-development indicates that the principles of our Saemaul projects are highly regarded.

New Zealand, which grew into one of the world's leading agricultural nations by developing mountainous terrain similar to Korea, is also said to be the result of the pioneering efforts of its residents.

In July 1971, the project performance up to that point was analyzed to establish a new direction for the movement. It was discovered that the performance of the pilot project was greater in villages that possessed competent, dedicated leaders and a strong sense of cooperation and development awareness among residents. Based on this, the principles of Saemaul Undong were defined as diligence, self-help, and cooperation, and the movement began to be deployed with an emphasis on spiritual unity and cooperation of residents rather than material growth. This was because the project's drive depended on residents eager for development, and as long as they united around a leader, the project's outcomes would be achieved.

Following the pilot stage, the direction of Saemaul Undong was established and systematized in 1972
70:
when it occurred. Even critics came to accept it as a wholesome national movement, and researchers and writers began to address rural development from their respective viewpoints. As a theoretical framework, the development process of Saemaul Undong was set to progress from ① environmental improvement and mental cultivation to ② income increase in rural cases. The direction of Saemaul Undong was also designed as a movement to be practiced not only by rural residents but by the entire population, thereby expanding from a rural development movement to a national movement.

There were criticisms that Saemaul Undong was government-led in its early stages and that government leadership was inappropriate. Although local administrative agencies were involved in planning, technology, and funding support during the pilot phase, efforts were made over time to transition to a civilian-led model except for financial support. Project execution was managed from the beginning by the Village Development Committee organized in each village, and in some villages, these organizations assumed responsibility for everything from planning to implementation.

In the early stages of the movement, the most difficult challenges were project planning, residents' technical skills for project execution, and leadership. A leader had to be highly trusted and possess strong leadership qualities, but even a qualified leader had to endure significant personal sacrifice. Development theory regarding training indicates that projects exceeding planning and technical capabilities must align with the residents' interests and capacities; even if a plan is well-designed, a low level of technical training among those executing the project can result in losses and fail to contribute significantly to improving residents' welfare. In the beginning, we repeatedly experienced such outcomes. This is why the Saemaul Leaders Training Institute was established to cultivate leaders and educate numerous residents through various technical training programs. Today, in villages with competent leaders, residents acquire the capability to execute both local and wide-area projects, provided they are motivated and supplied with the necessary materials or funds.

However, there is a critical need to train more successors to the leaders who manage the projects. Given their age group at the launch of the movement, the current leaders are now in their 30s or 40s. We must train successors to replace them and encourage them to remain in rural areas by providing profit incentives. According to a survey in 1979, some villages had no members or only a few members in their village youth clubs or Saemaul youth associations. In the 1990s, when the rural population is projected to reach approximately 20% of the total population, even more competent leaders will be required.

In this regard, if we summarize the concept of Saemaul Undong, it can be condensed into two aspects. One is the realization of the "Ri-in" movement as a spiritual revolution to reignite the minds of villagers, who have fallen into an exhausted state due to the long-standing decline of national power, into vibrant creativity. The other is a movement to actively translate the ideals of public welfare and seeking truth from facts, which flashed briefly during the Silhak movement and then faded, into modern scientific development and industrialization. Therefore, without conceiving a new order of the mind, the creation of a new village (spiritual revolution and modernization) cannot succeed. Renewing the order of the mind is possible not simply through indoctrination based on theory, but rather by inducing experiential empathy and holistic resonance through action and practice. In this sense, the numerous rural and urban Saemaul Undong leaders of this land are proud men of action and excellent practitioners who have triggered such empathy and resonance.

The modern capitalist spirit (industrialization + scientific development) has several characteristics. It is by these characteristics that the modernization of the West succeeded.

First, the spirit of capitalism implies that the attitude toward acquiring profit differs from that of the feudal era. That is, the spirit of modernization rejects the attitude that generally evaluates the pursuit of profit as a moral evil. This does not mean, however, that the spirit of Western modernization accepts uncontrolled, unlimited instincts and impulses as they are. On the contrary, the spirit of modernization transforms the spirit of profit-seeking into an ethos, namely, a vocational ethic. As seen in Benjamin Franklin, the symbol of the spirit of modernization, diligence, a simple and temperate lifestyle, and a prudent attitude toward life are highlighted as economic ethics for modernization and capitalization.

Second, because capitalism and industrialization—symbols of the modern spirit—legitimize the pursuit of profit as a reward for continuously performing rational economic behavior, economic actions based on strict discipline and training are required. Therefore, the distinction between adventurous profit-seeking and rational capitalism becomes clear.

Third, to conduct economic activities rationally under strict discipline, a generally universalized standard of values for life must be established. That is, the standards of economic activity must not vary according to status discrimination, blood ties, or regional ties. In other words, if the scale of economic activity and economic ethics differ according to blood ties, regional ties, and school ties, a rational life ethic cannot be established, and without it, modernization cannot succeed. As Max Weber pointed out, "internal morality" (Binnen-

If this occurs, it is difficult for the spirit of modernization to succeed. The implementation guidelines for Saemaul Undong established at this time were: first, it should be developed as an autonomous national movement in which both rural and urban populations participate. Second, to shift toward an income-increasing movement, a permanent foundation tailored to the capabilities of residents and regional characteristics must be established. Third, it must be developed as an organized practical movement to ensure that trial and error are avoided. Fourth, the institutional framework for policy implementation must also be strengthened. Thus, starting from 1973, a comprehensively systematized and sustainable direction for the movement was finally established. Even under the circumstances we faced ten years prior, modernization was the most urgent proposition, and distinct objectives had to be set. First, the purpose of citizens' spiritual enlightenment was to address the state of resignation caused by long-standing Confucian influence and poverty, as well as the confusion regarding our unique sense of identity due to the mixing of Western materialism and individualism. The goal was to establish a new outlook on life, work, and the state, and to create a new culture. In other words, at a time when our traditional spiritual culture centered on loyalty and filial piety was being overshadowed by foreign cultures, the spiritual enlightenment movement aimed to reclaim our heritage, construct a new spiritual culture, and awaken citizens to the mental attitude required under international circumstances.

## Chapter 2. Basic Spirit of Saemaul Undong

### Section 1. Guiding Ideology of Saemaul Undong

#### 1. Will for the Modernization of the Homeland

The issues of national integration and national development, which represent the two major tasks of national revitalization, are directly linked to the modernization of the homeland. Generally, in the second half of the 20th century, modernization emerged as a common task that newly independent nations, including Korea, had to resolve, and all have grappled with the grand proposition of modernization. Although utmost efforts are being made to achieve these goals as quickly and efficiently as possible, significant differences exist in the situational conditions of modernization each country faces, as well as in the capacity of their political systems to coordinate and absorb these changes.

These differences are expressed as conceptual questions of modernization regarding 'what' should be set as the scope or target in achieving the national goal of modernization, and as methodological questions of 'how' modernization should be carried out. They are also expressed as process-related questions regarding 'through what stages' modernization should be achieved using the defined concept and chosen method. In other words, countries differ in their answers to the questions of what modernization is, how it should be achieved, and through what process it should occur. Collectively, these issues are often understood as the question of what the 'modernization model' should be, or what model is best suited for modernizing newly independent nations. These inquiries are directly linked to the determination for modernizing the homeland that Saemaul Undong must pursue.

##### A. Content of Modernization

It was from the 1950s that the issue of modernization or the development of newly independent states began to attract significant attention from social scientists. Initially, the issue of modernization was equated with economic development, but gradually, it became apparent that economic development itself
76:
could not be easily achieved by focusing solely on economic factors. As a result, interest in modernization, which had been focused on economic development, began to pay attention to non-economic factors alongside purely economic ones. Thus, social development and political development were also problematized as prerequisites or parallel conditions for economic development. Consequently, the term modernization came to be used in a sense that encompasses all fields of economy, society, politics, and culture in its concept. In other words, the answer to 'what is modernized' can be defined as developing the political, economic, social, and cultural domains of a specific society or state.
Understanding the meaning of modernization in our context, political development is to indigenize democracy; economic and social development is to achieve a welfare state through industrialization; and cultural development is to overcome national division and achieve the promotion of a national culture based on five thousand years of history and tradition.

## B. Searching for Methods of Modernization
Defining the meaning of modernization in this way raises the methodological question of 'how then shall we achieve modernization?' It is necessary to shed light on various perspectives regarding the methods for modernization.
First, as a question raised in general theories on the modernization of developing countries, there is the issue of how to connect with past traditions. In other words, the choice lies between the path of rupture versus continuity: whether to pursue modernization in a state of rupture with the past, like the modernization of France, or to pursue it along a line of continuity with the past. This discussion has long been raised among Western scholars as a methodological model for pursuing modernization, with writers taking different positions. According to the views of scholars who argue that modernization must take place in rupture with the past, traditional society inherently contains elements that obstruct modernization. Therefore, unless these are removed, the pursuit of modernization will inevitably require a long period of time. This argument holds a major advantage in terms of its capacity to shorten the time required for modernization. In other words, since modernization is, in one aspect, a competition with already advanced countries in the global arena and a competition among newly independent nations in another aspect, for us, [methods] that shorten the time
77:
of modernization must be selected. Today, the relationship between developed nations and newly independent nations is often compared to a race between a diligent rabbit and a tortoise. The satire of 'eternal backwardness,' suggesting that the tortoise can never catch up with the advanced rabbit, is frequently invoked by scholars and politicians, highlighting how difficult it is to shorten the time required for modernization.

In the modernization path we face today, the influence of past bad habits is indeed substantial. The remnants of the so-called Yangban culture, which can be described as excessively authoritarian, serve as one example. Although most of these have been corrected due to the generalization of the rationalist spirit through Saemaul Undong, family ties, nepotism, and regionalism still pose obstacles to pursuing modernization. Even if eliminating these bad habits of traditional culture does not necessarily mean a complete break with the past, it must continue to be developed as a method and principle for promoting modernization.

On the other hand, there are disadvantages to choosing a modernization method based on a rupture with the past. Although rupture with the past has the advantage of shortening time, discarding pre-modern traditions all at once is bound to entail the potential for intense social confusion. Considering that the mass migration of rural populations to cities due to early industrialization remains a headache for nations promoting industrialization, a sudden break with the past risks destroying the social consensus as a whole. This disadvantage is particularly noteworthy in our case, where the homeland is divided. We cannot simply reach for the fruit of shortening time while ignoring the intentions of those who constantly wait for a period of chaos in South Korean society to entangle the entire Korean Peninsula in the red clutches of communism.

As such, in determining how to handle the issue of the past as a method for promoting modernization, it is difficult to simply choose one side. Nevertheless, since our situation does not allow us to sit idle and wear the label of 'eternal underdevelopment,' we must create our own method. If we are to secure the advantage of shortening time while preventing sudden social chaos caused by rupture, we must overcome this through an original method of Korean-style modernization. Reflecting on our society's modernization efforts thus far, this logical conclusion points to the Sae-
78:
maul Undong that can be described as the original modernization method that overcomes these contradictions.

Another perspective on the modernization method is the choice of strategy between the modernization of environment versus the modernization of human beings. Modernization essentially means living well. And living well refers to a democratic welfare society, meaning that all citizens lead a life of freedom and equality in an affluent environment. However, in the method of achieving this goal, a strategic choice is indeed required regarding whether humans or the environment should be modernized first. It is a well-known fact that this problematic situation is often expressed as 'should we fit the clothes to the body, or the body to the clothes?' or raised as the question of 'should democratization precede, or should industrialization precede?'

In reality, this issue has been a core task of Korean politics over the past 30 years. Since our country has championed an open society since its founding, the rapid development of modern mass media allowed Western contemporary ideas to be transmitted with virtually no time lag. Consequently, while the 'head' underwent rapid Westernization, the industrialization process failed to develop the 'physical strength' to support these incoming modern trends, leaving the head and body in a state of imbalance. Despite the reality that poverty enveloped our environment, the head attempted to imitate the thoughts of citizens in advanced nations, which frequently manifested in entirely bizarre social deviance. Examples include the so-called hippie culture or inappropriate leisure crazes. At the same time, young university students mistook Western freedom for our own, raising slogans of 'democratization' and thereby exacerbating social confusion. Even leaving aside the question of whether they acted with an understanding of the essential meaning of democracy, it goes without saying that they had absolutely no opportunity to properly digest and acquire the true meaning of democracy. To that extent, Korean-style democracy has not yet taken root.

The question of whether to fit the clothes to the body or the body to the clothes must presume an understanding of the Korean 'terrain' that points toward modernization. The modernization of newly independent states is often compared to a three-legged race where two runners have their ankles tied together. If the two runners'

thoughts differ and they take steps at different speeds, they will fall. This is the same principle as causing social conflict and friction along the path of modernization. Conversely, if the two runners' thoughts are aligned, they can reach the finish line smoothly and quickly.

Ultimately, the issue of modernization methods can only be overcome when there is a prerequisite understanding of our 'terrain.' The answer to the question of 'how' to achieve modernization can be given as 'in a manner suited to the Korean situation.' This means promoting industrialization and democratization on the coordinates of Korean-style industrialization and Korean-style democracy, and ultimately implementing a Korean-style democratic welfare society. The choice of such modernization methods must become one of the guiding principles that Saemaul Undong pursues.

### C. Development of Modernization-Promoting Elements

In promoting modernization, there is also the perspective of choice between exogenous and endogenous factors: whether to prioritize endogenous factors or to pay attention to exogenous factors such as science and technology. It is a well-known fact that, in the development of modern society, especially in the West, the central engine of modernization was science and technology. Science and technology performed a pivotal role in industrialization, based on which modern states were formed in Western society. In modernization, passing through the stage of industrialization, which is essential to achieving the goal of industrialization, is impossible without advanced science and technology. In this sense, the influence of exogenous elements on our modernization path is immense. However, the problem is that science and technology are neither obtained for free nor given away. For the developed nations that possess them, they serve as the sole means to enjoy their current advanced status indefinitely. Consequently, the exogenous factors essential to our modernization are bound to be transmitted by developed nations colored with ideologies of domination over developing countries. From this perspective, science and technology can be considered a nationalistic element in another sense. This is precisely why terms such as American nationalism or European nationalism are frequently used today. Therefore, when industrialization and modernization are carried out by relying on exogenous elements, the goals may be easily achieved by utilizing the accumulated science and technology of developed nations, but
80:
we cannot but accept the permanent domination of culture, and in another sense, the premise of being a permanent underdeveloped country.

On the other hand, choosing an endogenous method has the advantage of establishing an independent culture and tradition, but it requires a long time and national sacrifice. Nevertheless, what is truly important in modernization is the endogenous aspect. That is, while seeds may be brought from the outside, sprouts only grow in one's own soil, so endogenous factors must be the mainstay of modernization.

It is true that exogenous factors are also important elements of modernization. However, without the soil of self-generated, traditional culture, neither industrialization nor modernization is meaningful. The subject of modernization we aim for is the nation as the basic unit, and there is a proposition that it must take root in the cultural soil built by the nation. In this sense, modernization is referred to as the 'modernization of the homeland' and 'national revitalization.'

The answer to whether to prioritize exogenous or endogenous factors as the method of modernization can be replaced by the response that what we aim and target is the modernization of the homeland and the revitalization of the nation. Furthermore, the pressure exerted by exogenous factors must be resolved through relationships of equality or cooperation with developed nations, based on our independent strength.

### D. Stages of Modernization and Consciousness Revolution

In understanding the issue of modernization through concepts, methods, and processes, ultimately, presenting the path to modernization boils down to the question of through what stages, or processes, the goal is achieved. This is commonly referred to as the stages of modernization or the modernization process model. A precise understanding of the stages of the modernization of the homeland provides an important guiding direction, particularly when considering that Saemaul Undong must be promoted as part of the modernization movement.

Even among scholars in developed countries who study modernization issues, there has recently been skepticism regarding previous claims that the stages of modernization would follow a single direction through fixed stages or processes. This trend acknowledges that there are diverse paths to modernization. Nevertheless, directing modernization along a certain path holds significant meaning. This is much like the necessity of a blueprint prior to construction, and

## Chapter 2 The Basic Spirit of Saemaul Undong

It is for the same reason.

It is widely known that dividing the stages of modernization into four or five stages is the general classification method for the modernization of developing nations. Looking at the common characteristics of this general theory, there is consensus that the process of modernization must first involve the formation of a nation-state. Once this stage is passed, it enters the stage of achieving industrialization, and once industrialization is completed, it must ultimately develop toward the goal of an affluent or welfare society. A.F.K. Organski, an authority on the study of modernization models for developing nations, goes so far as to emphasize that this process of modernization is the path that advanced nations have invariably trodden, and that they had to go through arduous struggles and extremely rugged paths along that journey.

From this perspective, it is highly predictable that the process of the modernization of the homeland, which we aim for, will inevitably be an arduous path. To begin with, the goal of nation-state formation, which is pointed out as the first stage of modernization, remains an unresolved task for us. This situation gives rise to the paramount national goals of security and peaceful unification, and consequently to the proposition that the path toward the modernization of the homeland must directly lead to unification. The arduous struggle for unification is indeed a process of the modernization of the homeland that we must indispensably achieve, and this must also be an ideology directly linked to the ultimate goals of modernization, such as the goal of industrialization and the realization of a welfare society.

If we summarize the path to modernization from the perspective of its process, we are in a situation where all stages of modernization overlap. When understood in terms of the national demand for modernization, this reality presents us with the task of addressing the demands for unification, industrialization, and welfare—the goals of the various stages of modernization—almost simultaneously. Consequently, for us, the path to modernization is more rugged and arduous than for any other nation, and a strong will and perseverance to overcome it emerge as absolute requirements.

In our situation, where we have no choice but to simultaneously pursue the overcoming of division, industrialization, democratization, and the realization of a welfare society, the path of modernization is not without the possibility of facing both progress and crisis at the same time. Therefore, the direction of the modernization of the homeland requires the formulation of a comprehensive strategy capable of coping with
82:
these challenges. The consciousness base serves as the common denominator of such a strategy, and thus, the only alternative to overcome the crisis is to absorb and integrate the Korean situation in a development-oriented manner through a revolution of consciousness.

As a foundation oriented toward modernization, consciousness must be diverse in content yet integrated as a single whole. In other words, to prevent individual consciousnesses from clashing and creating discord, they need to be sublimated into a single, unified ideology. This unified ideology may manifest at times as a movement and at other times as an ideology, but in its essence, it must embody a revolution of the spirit.

The reason why the modernization of the homeland we have advocated must be pursued with a spiritual revolution as its backbone is that only the outcome of consciousness can generate the creative power to overcome the problems exposed in the methods or processes of promoting modernization.

The necessity of having a unified spirit in pursuing modernization can be explained by analogy to the law of contradiction (Mousun) from an ancient Chinese fable. Contradiction, meaning 'spear' and 'shield,' can be interpreted to mean that overlapping demands in modernization can cause friction and conflict with each other. In other words, since an all-powerful spear and an all-powerful shield carry mutually conflicting meanings, their initial respective powers of being all-powerful are opposed, inevitably losing their meaning. To take an example in the methodology of modernization, it is similar to the logical conclusion that the claim that industrialization is the shortcut to modernization and the claim that democratization is the shortcut to modernization are tasks that must be resolved simultaneously for us, yet can never be resolved at the same time. The way to overcome this logic of contradiction is to keep the all-powerful spear and the all-powerful shield from colliding while maintaining their respective powers. That is, if instead of two separate owners dividing the spear and the shield, one person possesses both the spear and the shield at the same time, a situation where one must block the spear with the shield or pierce the shield with the spear will never arise.

The spiritual revolution in modernization is based on the same theory. Industrialization and democratization should not be

divided among multiple owners to cause conflict, but rather, by absorbing them both into the consciousness of a single individual as a higher ideology of modernization, the stance of a single owner can be maintained. Any opposition or conflict that may arise on the path of modernization is not only difficult to resolve in its own essence, but even if one intends to adjust these conflicts, numerous difficulties are bound to arise. The question of choice, such as whether to construct a highway or to provide scholarships to college students, can be constantly discussed.

However, it is difficult to judge which option will ultimately shorten the path of modernization. While this issue of choice is indeed a task for policymakers, at the level of the citizens who receive it, both must be equally recognized as meaningful for modernization.

Otherwise, it will be difficult to overcome the obstacles that arise on the long and rugged path of modernization. Whether the direction of modernization prioritizes security, focuses on industrialization, or puts welfare first, it is a duty we must uphold, and we must never forget that it is the path to modernize our own homeland, not another's.

Here lies the necessity of a spiritual revolution as the soil for modernization, and this is the reason why Saemaul Undong, as a part of the modernization movement, must assume the character of a consciousness reform movement. The reason why a spiritual or consciousness revolution is the path to modernizing the homeland is that it serves as a source of vitality and nourishment on the rugged and arduous path of modernization.

## 2. Industrialization and Saemaul Undong

In achieving modernization, what is urgent is not establishing new institutions, but rather the task of building a rich and strong nation as soon as possible out of an impoverished homeland trapped in a vicious cycle. The slogan 'The shortcut to the modernization of the homeland is liberation from poverty' was expressed through President Park's strong will and determination in the early 1960s, and emerged as one of the leading ideologies of the Saemaul Undong in the 1970s. The Saemaul Undong, which aimed to overcome five thousand years of poverty and achieve a better life, blossomed as a rural modernization movement. Under the basic direction that transforming the roots of our
84:
people's poverty into the roots of abundance must begin in rural areas, rural modernization commenced with 'income-generating' projects and 'environmental improvement' projects, which subsequently developed into a modernization movement for the entire society.

Historically, humanity has constantly struggled against poverty, and it can be said that the vast majority of human beings have, in fact, lived in poverty. Liberation from poverty, which had long been regarded as an eternal curse on humanity, became possible only with the advent of modern history, when a few Western nations underwent changes in their industrial structures, commonly referred to as industrialization.

The nations where this wave of industrialization occurred were mostly Western societies centered around the Atlantic, representing only a very small fraction of humanity. Through steady efforts spanning the past two centuries, these nations have now almost completely escaped their historical state of poverty, and in this sense, they are referred to as advanced industrial nations.

However, from the perspective of world history, it is no exaggeration to say that the second wave of industrialization was uniquely confined to Japan. As is well known, Japan's industrialization process began nearly three centuries later than that of the Western Atlantic nations, but due to rapid, high-level growth following World War II, Japan recorded astonishing performance, placing it at the top tier even among the aforementioned advanced industrial nations.

Now, the question for the future is which country will initiate the third wave of industrialization in world history. Today, only a small number of countries can be said to have succeeded in industrializing, while the majority of the approximately 150 nations in the world remain either in a pre-industrial state or in the midst of the industrialization process. Therefore, the competition to become the protagonist of the third wave of industrialization is bound to be a fiercely cutthroat contest, and those who fail and fall behind will continue to fail to escape historical poverty, with an 'affluent life' remaining merely an object of vague longing.

### A. The Coordinates of Korean Industrialization

Generally, industrialization in newly independent nations is underpinned by an awareness of the problem of public poverty and the desire to demand its re
85:
## Chapter 2 The Basic Spirit of Saemaul Undong

solution. This indicates that the primary criterion for recognizing the goal or necessity of industrialization is based on economic poverty. From this perspective, industrialization, as one of the goals of modernization in newly independent nations, naturally places emphasis on the realistic resolution of urgent economic problems rather than on the realization of an ideal society.

However, despite the realistic circumstances of developing nations, where industrialization must be viewed as a matter of economic development to overcome poverty, the reasons it occupies a central position on the path of modernization are threefold:

First, for a 'developing nation' acutely aware of the severe wealth gap between advanced and developing countries, pursuing rapid economic development is the path to securing independence in the truest sense.
Second, economic development is an indispensable prerequisite for satisfying the numerous new expectations held in common by members of a society attempting to modernize, namely the improvement of living standards, the spread of education, and the promotion of healthcare.
Third, economic development is a fundamental element that brings about changes in values, motivation, and enthusiasm, which are essential to the modernization process.

Whether the necessity of industrialization stems from the realistic goal of liberation from poverty, or from the significance of securing independence, fulfilling new expectations, and developing values and motivations essential for modernization, the goals of industrialization must take into account the 'ground' (conditions) under which these desires and meanings can be put into practice. While the root cause of the backwardness of newly independent nations lies in the underdevelopment of their political, economic, and cultural structures, from an economic standpoint, it lies in the underdevelopment of the industrial sector, which is the secondary industry. It is impossible to hypothesize that all developing nations can satisfy their desire for liberation from poverty or their goals of modernization solely through industrialization. Since developing nations have historical, geographical, demographic, and cultural differences, it is necessary for each to select the direction and process of industrialization according to their respective conditions.

Furthermore, for newly independent nations that must pursue industrialization under circumstances different from the industrial background established by advanced nations, there is also a serious question of who should lead
86:
this process.

The difference between the initial period of industrialization in advanced nations and the 'ground' (conditions) faced by newly independent nations today becomes clearer when borrowing the words of Gunnar Myrdal: 'In most cases, newly independent nations have significantly lower economic levels, an unfavorable ratio of population to resources, and rapid population growth is an even worse condition. Furthermore, they lack outlets for emigration, do not possess international capital markets, and are greatly lagging in social institutional prerequisites such as traditions of rationality or laws. In addition, newly independent nations are latecomers following from behind, do not possess colonies to exploit as markets or sources of raw materials, and while the majority of the world's nations are agricultural, they also lack the advantage that advanced nations had in developing by enjoying quasi-monopolistic profits as the sole industrial nations.'

Taking the above discussions into consideration, achieving the goals of industrialization within the Korean context requires a prerequisite of accurate understanding of both the realistic desires of the public and the 'ground' (conditions).

Looking back at the fact that upon the establishment of the Republic of Korea, the Constitution prescribed participation and distribution rather than the economy as the primary national goals for modernization, it is evident that an error was made from the very beginning in recognizing the public desire for liberation from poverty.

Prior to accepting the realistic demand for industrialization, namely 'liberation from poverty,' there was an obsession with the fiction of Western-style political democracy, and it took more than 15 years to awaken from this illusion. Moreover, the flaws in power and economy arising from the lack of political development preceding mixed or public economies have forced the presentation of slogans such as 'social purification' and 'eradication of irregularities' as inevitable prerequisites of governance, even now, after more than 30 years.

The ultimate path to achieving the goals of industrialization lies in grounding ourselves in an accurate diagnosis of the public's desires and an understanding of the 'ground.' And this must be consolidated into an ideology oriented toward modernization.

B. The Rural Modernization Movement

Industrialization, as a process of modernizing the homeland, was launched in earnest based on national desires and the understanding of the situational context of Korea, in the form of a rural modernization
87:
## Chapter 2 The Basic Spirit of Saemaul Undong

movement in the 1970s, namely the Saemaul Undong. That the Saemaul Undong began at the specific time of the 1970s and with the rural area as its starting point was due to the legacy of the 1960s, along with a leader and a guiding ideology oriented toward the modernization of the homeland.

Consequently, the late President Park Chung-hee, who concluded in the early 1960s that the shortcut to modernization lay in liberation from poverty, faced the task of how and where to generate the power to escape poverty. According to the general logic of industrialization, developing nations must use agriculture as a base, develop it, and use the surplus generated to gradually undergo the process of industrialization. According to this method, for Korea to industrialize, the rural areas would have to toil and save, which would impose an unbearable burden on farmers, and only after a long time would the surplus for industrialization be generated. Given the geopolitical situation surrounding the Korean Peninsula in the 1960s, we did not have the luxury of time to follow such general theories, and we also had to bear the employment difficulty of finding jobs in the agricultural sector for the many college graduates produced every year. In this regard, we must note that in many Southeast Asian countries today, while the number of college graduates is increasing, the lack of jobs for them within the traditional rural economic base has even become a factor of social instability.

Under general economic theories on industrialization, Korea's poverty problem would have inevitably remained trapped in a fateful, unbreakable vicious cycle. However, the late President Park's firm conviction that the modernization of the homeland could not be achieved without escaping poverty, combined with his will to overcome it, led to the discovery of a breakthrough from this vicious cycle. The fruit of such will and determination was manifested in Korea's development during the 1960s. Indeed, the First and Second Five-Year Economic Development Plans of the 1960s, carried out amidst negative public opinion claiming 'it will not work' or 'it will be too difficult,' were expressions of the potential of the Korean people, emerging as proof of the 'can-do' spirit driven solely by the leader's strong will and determination.

The high economic growth achieved by the Korean economy in the 1960s was more pronounced in cities than in rural areas, and in non-agricultural sectors rather than in agriculture. However, as the foundation for industrialization was established, exports increased rapidly, and the volume of economic activity in commercial and industrial cities grew, the driving force to promote rural
88:
modernization was generated.

This potential enhanced the government's capacity to support agricultural and fishery village development. As government support for rural development increased year by year, the division between what the government should do and what the villagers had to do for themselves became clear.

Among some farmers, reliance on outside help increased as government support grew, but on the other hand, a farmer's spirit—that rural areas could only modernize if they did their own work themselves—arose, and self-reliance movements began to spring up here and there. This phenomenon became prominent by the late 1960s.

This fact indicates that while the first impetus for rural modernization in Korea was created in the process of industrializing the Korean economy, as the potential gained from industrialization flowed into rural areas, the second impetus for rural modernization arose from within rural areas by the farmers themselves. The permanent and creative force for rural modernization is, after all, the power of self-reliance generated by the farmers themselves.

It can be said that the late President Park's firm will and determination for the modernization of the homeland were the direct driving force that ignited the passion for Saemaul in the hearts of the farmers.

Along with the leader's patriotism and determination to build an affluent homeland, the passion for Saemaul, in which men and women of all ages participated to make their own hometowns better places to live through their own efforts, spread like wildfire across the nation.

The Saemaul spirit of diligence, self-help, and cooperation was a direct reflection of the farming spirit.

This farming spirit is indeed the love for farming and the love for one's hometown. Agriculture, by nature, cannot be done by others but must be carried out by the farmers themselves; farming cannot succeed without diligence; and because falsehood does not work in farming against nature, one has no choice but to be sincere. Since farms are small-scale, only frugality—making a mountain out of dust—is the way to increase family assets, and rural life inherently requires cooperation in the form of mutual aid among neighbors.

Therefore, in our countryside, where such a spirit has been cultivated for thousands of years, the spirit of self-help, self-reliance, diligence, sincerity, frugality, and cooperation has been passed down as the farming spirit. However, such a farming spirit had been fading in recent centuries under the influence of transitional
